items.title: Hunger, satiety, and eating behavior after craniopharyngioma - narrative review on current management and future therapeutic perspectives.
items.summary: This narrative review synthesizes evidence on eating behavior and hypothalamic obesity in craniopharyngioma patients, identifying a striking gap: only 10 of 82 included studies used validated eating-behavior measures, and eating behavior was rarely a primary outcome. Across the literature, setmelanotide — an MC4R agonist — emerged as the only intervention in a randomized controlled trial to specifically target hyperphagia and achieve significant weight reduction in craniopharyngioma-related obesity. The authors emphasize that without long-term studies using standardized tools, the mechanistic drivers of hyperphagia in this population (e.g., loss of satiety signaling, altered reward circuitry) remain incompletely characterized, limiting both diagnosis and treatment optimization.
items.caveat: Narrative review methodology introduces selection bias, and the evidence base for setmelanotide is based on limited RCT data in a rare population. Generalizability across childhood-onset versus adult-onset craniopharyngioma is unclear, and long-term safety data for MC4R agonists in this context remain limited.
items.quiz_question: A 19-year-old with a history of childhood craniopharyngioma treated with surgery and radiotherapy presents with severe, unrelenting hyperphagia and progressive obesity (BMI 42 kg/m²) despite dietary counseling and GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy. Which pharmacologic mechanism has the strongest current RCT-level evidence for directly targeting hyperphagia in this setting?
items.quiz_answer: Melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R) agonism with setmelanotide is supported by the only identified RCT demonstrating successful targeting of hyperphagia and significant weight loss in craniopharyngioma-related obesity, reflecting the downstream loss of hypothalamic MC4R signaling in these patients.

items.title: Comparing machine learning algorithms for predicting postoperative medical management in prolactinoma surgery: a nested cross-validation study.
items.summary: This retrospective single-center study of 138 patients who underwent surgical prolactinoma resection used nested cross-validation to evaluate eight ML algorithms for predicting which patients would require postoperative dopamine agonist therapy (DAT), affecting roughly half the cohort. A parsimonious five-feature model—preoperative prolactin, tumor volume, FSH, maximum diameter, and prolactin density—achieved an AUROC of ~0.78–0.79 across the best-performing algorithms, with only a modest gain over a conventional logistic regression baseline (AUROC 0.735). SHAP analysis identified elevated preoperative prolactin, larger tumor volume, and lower FSH as the primary drivers. The authors appropriately call for external multicenter validation before clinical implementation.
items.caveat: Single-center retrospective design with 138 patients limits generalizability, and the modest incremental gain over simple logistic regression raises questions about whether the added complexity of ML is warranted; external validation is essential.
items.quiz_question: A 35-year-old woman undergoes transsphenoidal resection of a prolactinoma with a preoperative prolactin of 420 ng/mL, tumor volume 4.2 cm³, and suppressed FSH. According to this study's five-feature predictive model, which direction would her SHAP-driven risk estimate lean regarding postoperative dopamine agonist requirement?
items.quiz_answer: Her profile—elevated preoperative prolactin, larger tumor volume, and low FSH—represents the three primary drivers associated with higher predicted probability of requiring postoperative dopamine agonist therapy, per the SHAP analysis in this study.

items.title: Elevated IGF-1 levels are associated with accelerated bone age advancement during growth hormone therapy in children: a multicenter cohort study.
items.summary: This multicenter registry study of 1,944 children (idiopathic GHD, idiopathic short stature, or SGA) found that each 1-SD increase in IGF-1 SDS during GH therapy was independently associated with a 24% higher risk of bone age advancement (BA/CA >1). Children born SGA were at significantly higher risk than those with IGHD (HR 2.15), and ISS patients also showed elevated risk (HR 1.63). Findings were consistent across sex, age subgroups, and a stricter BA/CA >1.2 sensitivity analysis, supporting individualized GH dosing with close IGF-1 and skeletal monitoring.
items.caveat: Observational registry design precludes causal inference; bone age assessment carries inherent inter-reader variability, and the study does not report final adult height outcomes, which are the clinically meaningful endpoint.
items.quiz_question: An 8-year-old girl born SGA is 6 months into GH therapy. Her IGF-1 SDS has risen from +0.5 to +2.8. Based on this study's findings, how should you counsel the family about bone maturation risk, and what monitoring adjustment is warranted?
items.quiz_answer: SGA status and a rising IGF-1 SDS are both independently associated with accelerated bone age advancement in this study. The family should be counseled about this risk, and dose reduction to target an IGF-1 SDS within the normal range, combined with more frequent bone age radiographs, would be the monitoring adjustment supported by these findings.

items.title: [Oral urea in the management of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion syndrome associated with Guillain-Barré syndrome, severe dysautonomia, and pheochromocytoma ‒ An exceptional clinical case].
items.summary: This case report describes an 82-year-old man with pheochromocytoma and colon adenocarcinoma who developed SIADH in the setting of Guillain-Barré syndrome with severe dysautonomia, a combination that severely constrained conventional hyponatremia therapies such as fluid restriction and oral sodium chloride. Oral urea achieved safe, gradual sodium correction without significant adverse events, enabling completion of preoperative preparation and successful subsequent adrenalectomy and colonic resection. The authors note this appears to be the first reported use of oral urea for SIADH in a patient with concurrent pheochromocytoma and Guillain-Barré-related dysautonomia.
items.caveat: Single case report; no generalizable efficacy or safety data. Pheochromocytoma was presumably not causing the SIADH, but the interaction between catecholamine excess, dysautonomia, and sodium homeostasis in this scenario is complex and the report cannot isolate the contribution of each condition.
items.quiz_question: A patient with a known pheochromocytoma awaiting adrenalectomy develops symptomatic SIADH (Na 126 mEq/L) in the context of severe autonomic instability. Fluid restriction is poorly tolerated and oral NaCl is ineffective. What alternative oral agent does this case report support, and what is its mechanism of action in SIADH?
items.quiz_answer: Oral urea is the agent described. It acts as an osmotic agent, increasing free water excretion by the kidneys without significantly affecting sodium or potassium, thereby raising serum sodium gradually and safely—particularly useful when vasopressin receptor antagonists or aggressive fluid restriction are impractical.

items.title: Acromegalic Osteoarthropathy: A New Paradigm of Pathological Musculoskeletal Remodeling.
items.summary: This review proposes an integrative framework repositioning acromegalic musculoskeletal disease—traditionally treated as separate complications of skeletal fragility and arthropathy—as a unified disorder of pathological musculoskeletal remodeling involving bone, joints, muscle, and body composition. The authors argue that bone fragility, arthropathy, muscle dysfunction, and altered body composition share common biological mechanisms driven by GH/IGF-1 excess, and that these changes frequently persist even after successful biochemical remission. Practically, the review advocates shifting from endocrine-centered care to phenotype-driven, multidisciplinary surveillance with attention to fracture risk determinants beyond BMD.
items.caveat: This is a narrative review without systematic meta-analysis or new primary data; recommendations for practice change remain expert-opinion level pending prospective longitudinal studies.
items.quiz_question: A 52-year-old woman with acromegaly achieves biochemical remission (normal IGF-1) after transsphenoidal surgery. She reports progressive knee pain and back stiffness. Her DEXA is borderline normal. How should her musculoskeletal status be managed going forward?
items.quiz_answer: According to this framework, biochemical remission does not halt acromegalic musculoskeletal remodeling; arthropathy, vertebral fractures, and muscle dysfunction can persist or progress independently. She warrants ongoing phenotype-driven surveillance including vertebral fracture assessment, arthropathy evaluation, and functional muscle assessment—not reassurance based on BMD or IGF-1 alone.

items.title: From Detection to Decision: A Single-Center Analysis of Preoperative Imaging, Surgical Indications and Postoperative Histopathological Findings in Adrenal Lesions.
items.summary: In this retrospective series of 157 adrenalectomy patients, 9% of lesions ≥4 cm and 14% of lesions ≥6 cm were malignant on final pathology; notably, the malignancy rate rose to 22% for right-sided lesions ≥6 cm. All adrenocortical carcinomas exceeded 4 cm (mean 8.3 cm) and occurred exclusively on the right side in this cohort. Tumor size and right-sided localization were independently associated with malignancy on logistic regression, reinforcing current guideline thresholds while adding laterality as a potential clinical signal.
items.caveat: Single-center retrospective design with 157 patients limits generalizability; the exclusive right-sided distribution of ACC may reflect selection/referral bias rather than a true biological predilection. The absence of imaging HU data and washout characteristics limits radiologic correlation.
items.quiz_question: A 61-year-old man is referred for a right adrenal mass measuring 6.5 cm with HU 28 on non-contrast CT and indeterminate washout. He has no symptoms of hormone excess, but screening labs reveal mildly elevated 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines. Based on this study's findings, what is the approximate malignancy risk for a right-sided lesion ≥6 cm, and what are the management implications?
items.quiz_answer: This study found a 22% malignancy rate for right-sided adrenal lesions ≥6 cm. Combined with indeterminate imaging characteristics and biochemical evidence of catecholamine excess (pheo must be excluded and treated first), surgical resection after appropriate alpha-blockade is strongly warranted—both to exclude/treat pheochromocytoma and to address the meaningful malignancy risk.

items.title: Treatment of growth hormone deficiency with long-acting growth hormones in children, adolescents and adults: Clinical evidence and practical considerations.
items.summary: This review synthesizes clinical trial evidence for three once-weekly long-acting GH (LAGH) formulations now available in the EU—lonapegsomatropin, somatrogon, and somapacitan—all of which demonstrated non-inferiority to daily GH in annualized height velocity in children, with comparable safety profiles. Somapacitan is currently the only LAGH approved in France for both pediatric and adult GHD, making it the most clinically versatile option across the age spectrum. The review addresses practical dosing, monitoring, transition-period management, and special populations, highlighting that real-world adherence data and long-term metabolic outcomes remain under active study.
items.caveat: Pivotal trials establishing non-inferiority were primarily growth velocity endpoints in children; long-term metabolic, bone health, and quality-of-life data for adults on LAGHs are limited and ongoing. Some trial data are industry-sponsored. EU approvals differ from other regulatory jurisdictions (e.g., FDA).
items.quiz_question: A 14-year-old with childhood-onset GHD and documented poor adherence to daily GH injections is transitioning to adult care. His parents ask about once-weekly GH options. What does current clinical trial evidence show regarding efficacy of LAGH formulations compared to daily GH in children, and what is the key remaining evidence gap?
items.quiz_answer: Clinical trials of once-weekly LAGHs (lonapegsomatropin, somatrogon, somapacitan) have demonstrated non-inferiority to daily GH for annualized height velocity in children with comparable safety. The key remaining evidence gap is long-term real-world data on metabolic outcomes, bone health, and sustained adherence benefits—particularly relevant during the transition to adult care.

items.title: Pheochromocytoma Masquerading as Acute Coronary Syndrome Complicated by Cardiogenic Shock: A CARE-Compliant Case Report.
items.summary: This case report describes a 59-year-old man with a 10-year history of intermittent chest tightness who presented with acute cardiogenic shock, elevated troponin, and significantly reduced LVEF, but no obstructive coronary disease on angiography (MINOCA pattern). Plasma free normetanephrine and metanephrine were markedly elevated (>630–680× ULN), and CT confirmed a right adrenal mass. Following two weeks of alpha-blockade with phenoxybenzamine and volume expansion, laparoscopic adrenalectomy was performed, with complete normalization of cardiac function postoperatively, confirming catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy as the mechanism.
items.caveat: Single case report; the degree of metanephrine elevation here was extreme, and clinicians should note that biochemical confirmation may be more subtle in other cases of pheo-induced cardiomyopathy. The reversibility of catecholamine cardiomyopathy is well established but not universal.
items.quiz_question: A 62-year-old man presents with acute cardiogenic shock, troponin elevation, and reduced LVEF on echo, but coronary angiography shows no significant stenosis. Blood pressure has been labile for years. What is the next most critical diagnostic step before attributing this to a primary cardiomyopathy?
items.quiz_answer: Measurement of plasma free metanephrines (or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines) to exclude pheochromocytoma, followed by adrenal CT if biochemistry is positive. As illustrated in this case, pheo can present as MINOCA with cardiogenic shock, and missing the diagnosis risks a fatal catecholamine crisis during further cardiac interventions.
items.journal: The American journal of case reports

items.title: Deep Learning Based on Magnetic Resonance Imaging for Preoperative Prediction of Pituitary Neuroendocrine Tumors Subtypes.
items.summary: This retrospective two-center study of 888 patients with pathologically confirmed PitNETs trained a YOLOv11 deep learning model on standard preoperative MRI sequences to classify tumors into four molecular lineage groups (PIT1, TPIT, SF1, and no distinct lineage). Sagittal contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging performed best (mAP50-95: 0.901), with robust performance across internal, temporal external, and multicenter validation cohorts. If prospectively validated, this approach could enable noninvasive preoperative molecular subtyping to guide surgical and adjuvant treatment planning before histopathology is available.
items.caveat: Retrospective design with no prospective validation; model performance metrics are promising but mAP is an object-detection metric not directly equivalent to clinical diagnostic accuracy measures like AUC or sensitivity/specificity. Generalizability beyond the two contributing centers is unproven.
items.quiz_question: A 48-year-old woman with a nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma is scheduled for transsphenoidal resection. Her surgical team asks whether preoperative MRI alone can reliably predict the tumor's transcription factor lineage (e.g., SF1 vs. PIT1). Based on this study, what can you tell them?
items.quiz_answer: Deep learning models applied to standard preoperative MRI sequences — particularly sagittal contrast-enhanced T1WI — showed high accuracy for molecular subtype classification in retrospective cohorts, with mAP50-95 of up to 0.901. However, this remains investigational; prospective validation is needed before MRI-based subtyping can replace or guide postoperative immunohistochemical lineage classification in routine practice.

items.title: Hyponatremia as the Initial Presentation of Rathke's Cleft Cyst-Related Hypopituitarism.
items.summary: This case report highlights a 76-year-old woman presenting with severe euvolemic hyponatremia (without headache or visual symptoms) as the sole initial manifestation of pan-hypopituitarism caused by a Rathke's cleft cyst with mild suprasellar extension. Secondary adrenal insufficiency was identified as the driver of hyponatremia; hydrocortisone replacement led to sodium normalization, underscoring that untreated central adrenal insufficiency — rather than AVP excess alone — can be the primary mechanism. The case reinforces that pituitary MRI and a full anterior pituitary hormone panel are warranted in any euvolemic hyponatremia workup that lacks an obvious cause.
items.caveat: Single case report; the relative contributions of central hypothyroidism versus secondary adrenal insufficiency to the hyponatremia were not formally separated. Mild hyperprolactinemia from stalk compression was also present, adding complexity to interpretation.
items.quiz_question: A 78-year-old woman presents with Na of 126 mEq/L, clinically euvolemic, no diuretics, TSH normal per primary care records. Urine osmolality is 420 mOsm/kg and urine Na is 55 mEq/L — consistent with SIADH. She has no headache or visual complaints. What additional evaluation should be performed before labeling this as idiopathic SIADH?
items.quiz_answer: A morning cortisol (and if borderline, a cosyntropin stimulation test) plus a full anterior pituitary hormone panel (free T4, LH/FSH, IGF-1, prolactin) and pituitary MRI should be obtained. As this case illustrates, secondary adrenal insufficiency from an occult sellar lesion such as a Rathke's cleft cyst can present as apparent SIADH, and glucocorticoid replacement — not fluid restriction — is the corrective intervention.

items.title: Infiltrative and inflammatory systemic disorders involving the pituitary gland.
items.summary: This comprehensive review systematically covers the full spectrum of infiltrative and inflammatory disorders affecting the hypothalamic-pituitary region, including granulomatous, histiocytic, infectious, neoplastic, and autoimmune/hypophysitis etiologies. A key practical framework is offered for neuroimaging interpretation: symmetric stalk/gland enlargement with homogeneous enhancement favors lymphocytic, IgG4-related, or granulomatous hypophysitis, while rim enhancement, necrosis, or bone-destructive changes should prompt consideration of infectious or neoplastic causes. The authors emphasize that arginine vasopressin deficiency with pituitary stalk thickening is highly suggestive of a non-adenomatous lesion, and that a structured diagnostic work-up—incorporating targeted labs, hormonal evaluation, and histopathology when needed—should precede empiric immunosuppression or surgery. Importantly, two parallel management tracks are stressed: urgent corticotroph axis replacement and etiology-specific therapy.
items.caveat: This is a narrative review without systematic methodology or meta-analysis; the imaging pattern rules described, while clinically useful, are generalizations with meaningful overlap across etiologies and should not replace multidisciplinary judgment.
items.quiz_question: A 45-year-old woman presents with polyuria, fatigue, and headache. MRI shows a thickened pituitary stalk with symmetric, homogeneously enhancing enlargement of the stalk and posterior pituitary. Hormonal evaluation confirms central diabetes insipidus and secondary adrenal insufficiency. What diagnosis should you most strongly consider, and what is the most urgent initial management step?
items.quiz_answer: Symmetric stalk/gland enlargement with homogeneous enhancement strongly suggests lymphocytic hypophysitis, IgG4-related hypophysitis, or granulomatous disease (e.g., sarcoidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis). The most urgent initial step is glucocorticoid replacement for corticotroph deficiency, which can be life-threatening; DDAVP for diabetes insipidus should follow. A targeted systemic work-up (ACE, IgG4, chest imaging, metabolic screen) should be initiated before empiric immunosuppression.

items.title: Prolactinoma assessment and management: an international multidisciplinary cross-sectional survey of current practice.
items.summary: This international survey of 249 clinicians (210 endocrinologists, 39 neurosurgeons) across four continents mapped real-world prolactinoma practice against the 2023 Pituitary Society Consensus Statement. Despite guidelines supporting surgery as an equal first-line option in selected microprolactinomas, cabergoline remained overwhelmingly preferred in that setting. Only 20% of respondents routinely referred newly diagnosed cases for multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussion, and resource gaps were notable—including inconsistent Knosp grade reporting and limited access to transcription factor immunohistochemistry. Neurosurgeons varied considerably on indications for surgery and views on dopamine agonist-induced tumor fibrosis.
items.caveat: Survey-based data are subject to response bias, and self-reported practice may not accurately reflect actual clinical behavior; the neurosurgeon sample (n=39) is small and may not be representative internationally.
items.quiz_question: According to the 2023 Pituitary Society Consensus Statement, surgery is considered an equal first-line option in selected cases of microprolactinoma. However, this survey found that most clinicians still preferred cabergoline in that scenario. For which patient profile might surgery be a genuinely preferred first-line option over dopamine agonist therapy in a microprolactinoma?
items.quiz_answer: Per the 2023 Pituitary Society guidance (as reflected in this survey's framing), surgery may be preferred as first-line in selected microprolactinomas in patients who desire definitive cure and wish to avoid long-term medical therapy, those planning pregnancy who want to minimize drug exposure, or those intolerant of or non-adherent to dopamine agonists—provided the surgery is performed at an experienced center with acceptable cure rates for microadenomas.

items.title: The Sentinel Hormone GDF-15, Glucocorticoid Homeostasis and Adrenal Disorders.
items.summary: This review in Endocrine Reviews synthesizes emerging evidence that growth and differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15), a stress-responsive hormone signaling via the brainstem GFRAL receptor, interacts dynamically with the HPA axis. The authors propose that GDF-15 may act as a "sentinel hormone" capable of activating the HPA axis during cellular stress, with downstream glucocorticoid signaling potentially mediating some of GDF-15's known cardiovascular, metabolic, immune, and musculoskeletal effects. Additionally, the review discusses putative roles for GDF-15 in adrenal insufficiency (including as a biomarker or modifier of glucocorticoid replacement adequacy) and in adrenocortical carcinoma biology.
items.caveat: This is a mechanistic and hypothesis-generating review; the proposed GDF-15–HPA axis interplay is largely based on preclinical and associative data, and no clinical trials or interventional data in adrenal disease are yet available. Findings should be interpreted as preliminary until prospective clinical studies are conducted.
items.quiz_question: A patient with known adrenal insufficiency on stable glucocorticoid replacement presents with unexplained weight loss, fatigue, and nausea. GDF-15 levels are markedly elevated. Based on the framework proposed in this review, what additional considerations does elevated GDF-15 raise in the context of HPA axis disease?
items.quiz_answer: According to this review, elevated GDF-15 in a patient with adrenal insufficiency could reflect ongoing cellular stress and may signal inadequate glucocorticoid replacement or an intercurrent stress state activating the HPA axis. GDF-15 signals via GFRAL to suppress appetite and induce nausea/vomiting—symptoms that can mimic adrenal crisis or under-replacement. The review also raises the hypothesis that GDF-15 itself may modulate HPA axis activity, so elevated levels warrant reassessment of replacement adequacy and investigation for intercurrent illness, while recognizing the clinical evidence base remains preliminary.

items.title: Endocrine and surgical outcomes after medial cavernous sinus wall resection for functioning pituitary adenomas: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies (493 patients) found that intentional medial cavernous sinus wall resection (MCSWR) was associated with pooled endocrine remission rates of 87% for acromegaly, 89% for Cushing's disease, and 78% for prolactinomas, with gross total resection achieved in 92% overall. Recurrence occurred in only 6% at follow-up, and serious complications were rare — no ICA injuries, cranial nerve palsies in 3%, and CSF leak in 4%. These data suggest MCSWR is a viable surgical strategy for cavernous sinus-invasive functioning adenomas in experienced hands, with an acceptable safety profile.
items.caveat: The evidence base is predominantly retrospective, single-arm, and from high-volume centers, with follow-up ranging from only 9–30 months in most cohorts — insufficient to capture late recurrences. Risk of bias was rated serious to critical in most studies, and the absence of comparative controls limits causal inference.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old woman with Cushing's disease has a 12 mm corticotroph adenoma with radiologic evidence of medial cavernous sinus wall invasion (Knosp grade 2). Her surgeon is considering medial cavernous sinus wall resection. Based on the best available aggregate data, what remission rate and major complication rate should she be counseled about?
items.quiz_answer: Based on this meta-analysis, the pooled endocrine remission rate for Cushing's disease after MCSWR is approximately 89%, with a recurrence rate of ~6%. Major complication rates are low: ICA injury 0%, CN III/VI palsies ~3% each, and postoperative CSF leak ~4%. However, she should be informed these data come from high-volume, largely retrospective series with limited follow-up.

items.title: Adrenal suppression secondary to inhaled corticosteroids.
items.summary: This Canadian Pediatric Society position statement addresses the underrecognized risk of adrenal suppression (AS) from inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) in children, which can be life-threatening despite being a 'topical' therapy. The Working Group recommends screening with a morning serum cortisol in asymptomatic children on high-dose ICS for ≥3 months, any ICS dose combined with a CYP3A4 inhibitor, or in any child with symptoms of AS regardless of dose. Pediatric Endocrinology referral is warranted when morning cortisol is low or clinical suspicion is high, with individualized optimization of ICS technique, dosing, and comorbidity management to minimize AS risk.
items.caveat: This is a guideline/position statement rather than a primary research study, so it reflects expert consensus and existing evidence rather than new trial data. Specific cortisol threshold cutoffs for 'low' are not defined in the abstract, requiring clinician judgment and local laboratory reference ranges.
items.quiz_question: A 9-year-old with moderate-persistent asthma is on high-dose fluticasone via MDI for 6 months and is also receiving itraconazole (a CYP3A4 inhibitor) for tinea capitis. He is currently asymptomatic. According to Canadian Pediatric Society recommendations, what is the appropriate next step?
items.quiz_answer: This child meets two screening criteria — high-dose ICS for ≥3 months AND concurrent CYP3A4 inhibitor use. A morning serum cortisol should be obtained regardless of symptoms. If the result is low or clinical suspicion remains high, Pediatric Endocrinology referral is indicated.

items.title: xsCT-based radiomics for adrenal incidentaloma characterization.
items.summary: This retrospective single-center study of 135 patients developed CT-based radiomic models to distinguish benign (adenoma, myelolipoma, ganglioneuroma, pseudocyst) from malignant (pheochromocytoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, metastasis, lymphoma) adrenal incidentalomas. Using LASSO-selected radiomic features from non-contrast and portal-phase acquisitions, the models achieved AUCs of 0.88 and 0.84, respectively, suggesting meaningful discriminatory performance beyond traditional HU thresholds alone. This adds to growing evidence that radiomics could augment — though not yet replace — standard imaging characterization of adrenal masses.
items.caveat: Retrospective, single-center design with modest sample size (n=135) and no external validation cohort, substantially limiting generalizability. Notably, pheochromocytoma was classified as 'malignant' in the grouping scheme, which differs from standard clinical classification frameworks and may complicate direct application to routine practice.
items.quiz_question: A 55-year-old man has a 3.2 cm adrenal mass with unenhanced attenuation of 18 HU (indeterminate by standard criteria). A radiomic model applied to his CT images classifies it as 'high risk for malignancy.' How should this radiomic output be integrated into clinical decision-making based on current evidence?
items.quiz_answer: Radiomic models for adrenal incidentalomas show promising discriminatory performance (AUC ~0.88 in this study) but remain preliminary tools validated only in single-center retrospective cohorts without external validation. The radiomic result should be considered adjunctive information alongside standard evaluation — biochemical workup (metanephrines, aldosterone/renin, 1mg DST) and established imaging criteria — rather than as a standalone decision driver. Multidisciplinary discussion or referral to adrenal-focused centers is appropriate for indeterminate lesions.

items.title: Plasma cortisol cut-off concentrations using the dexamethasone suppression test in patients with adrenal incidentalomas.
items.summary: In this prospective cross-sectional study of 108 patients with adrenal incidentalomas and 101 matched controls, the guideline-recommended 50 nmol/L post-1mg DST cortisol threshold corresponded only to the 90th percentile of control values—not the 97.5th percentile as would be expected for a specificity-optimized cutoff. Using the control-derived 97.5th percentile threshold of 66 nmol/L (LC-MS/MS), the proportion classified as having autonomous cortisol secretion fell from 44% to 26%. Pre-DST ACTH was a poor predictor of post-DST cortisol suppression (AUC 0.69), and post-DST cortisol was not significantly associated with cardiometabolic comorbidities in this cohort.
items.caveat: Single-center cross-sectional design with a relatively modest sample size; LC-MS/MS and immunoassay results may not be directly interchangeable across institutions, and the clinical consequences of reclassifying patients at the higher threshold require prospective outcome data before any guideline revision is warranted.
items.quiz_question: A 58-year-old woman with an incidentally discovered 2.1 cm left adrenal adenoma (10 HU on non-contrast CT) undergoes a 1 mg overnight DST with post-DST cortisol of 58 nmol/L by immunoassay. Per current ESE/ENS@T guidelines she is classified as having mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS). Based on this new study's findings, what concern does this classification raise, and what does the data suggest about the 50 nmol/L threshold?
items.quiz_answer: The 50 nmol/L threshold corresponds to only the 90th percentile of a healthy control population rather than the conventional 97.5th percentile used to define pathological suppression failure—meaning it may overcall MACS. The study found that using a control-derived 66 nmol/L threshold (97.5th percentile by LC-MS/MS) reclassifies approximately 18% fewer patients as having autonomous secretion. This patient's result of 58 nmol/L falls below 66 nmol/L, raising the possibility that she would not meet a specificity-optimized threshold, though the clinical implications of reclassification remain to be validated prospectively.

items.title: Cardiovascular Morbidity in Acromegaly during a Long-term Follow-Up - a Nationwide Cohort Study.
items.summary: This Finnish nationwide retrospective cohort study (n=565 acromegaly patients, n=5,629 controls; median follow-up 17.2 years) demonstrates that cardiovascular morbidity in acromegaly begins years before diagnosis and remains persistently elevated throughout follow-up (HR 1.59 vs. controls). The highest excess risk was seen for pulmonary arterial disease (HR 2.74), valvular disease/cardiomyopathy (HR 2.68), and hypertension (HR 2.11). Crucially, even patients achieving biochemical remission after surgery with normal pituitary function still had significantly higher cardiovascular morbidity than controls, underscoring that cure does not normalize long-term cardiovascular risk.
items.caveat: Retrospective design with inherent selection and ascertainment biases; radiotherapy exposure and hypopituitarism were independently associated with increased CV morbidity, making it difficult to fully disentangle disease-intrinsic from treatment-related risk. Contemporary somatostatin analog use patterns are not granularly reported.
items.quiz_question: A 45-year-old man with acromegaly underwent successful transsphenoidal surgery 5 years ago and has maintained normal IGF-1 levels and intact pituitary function since. He asks whether his cardiovascular risk is now equivalent to the general population. What does this nationwide Finnish cohort study indicate?
items.quiz_answer: Despite biochemical remission and preserved pituitary function after surgery, this cohort study found that acromegaly patients continued to have significantly elevated cardiovascular morbidity compared to matched controls throughout the entire follow-up period (median >17 years). Excess risk for valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, pulmonary arterial disease, and hypertension persisted even in surgically cured patients, indicating that long-term cardiovascular surveillance and risk factor management remain essential regardless of biochemical cure.

items.title: A case report of a composite pheochromocytoma that occurred 13 years after adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma.
items.summary: In this retrospective single-center cohort of 120 patients with bilateral adrenal incidentalomas (BAIs) followed for at least 36 months, 56% had mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) at baseline and 44% were non-functioning. Among initially non-functioning BAIs, 32.1% developed MACS during follow-up (biochemical progression), while 44.3% showed radiological progression (≥3 mm increase in number or size). Importantly, radiological and biochemical progression were largely discordant—only 7.4% of radiologically progressing patients also showed biochemical progression—highlighting that BAIs may require individualized reassessment strategies beyond current ESE/ENS@T guidelines, which lack specific BAI-directed recommendations.
items.caveat: Retrospective single-center design with significant attrition (only 64/120 completed full biochemical follow-up); heterogeneous baseline characteristics and lack of a prospective comparator limit generalizability. The clinical consequences of biochemical progression (e.g., cardiometabolic outcomes) were not assessed.
items.quiz_question: A 67-year-old woman is referred for bilateral adrenal nodules (right 18 mm, left 14 mm), both with Hounsfield units <10 on unenhanced CT. Her 1 mg DST cortisol is 1.3 µg/dL (non-functioning). She asks whether she needs ongoing follow-up. What does this cohort study suggest about the natural history of non-functioning BAIs?
items.quiz_answer: This study found that approximately one-third (32.1%) of patients with initially non-functioning BAIs developed mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) over a minimum 36-month follow-up. Additionally, 44.3% showed radiological progression, and notably, biochemical and radiological progression were largely discordant events. These findings suggest that non-functioning BAIs cannot be safely discharged after a single normal evaluation, and support individualized clinical reassessment—though optimal surveillance intervals remain to be defined by prospective multicenter studies.

items.title: Progression of bilateral adrenal incidentalomas: a monocentric cohort study.
items.summary: In this retrospective single-center cohort of 120 patients with bilateral adrenal incidentalomas (BAIs) followed for at least 36 months, 32% of initially non-functioning lesions developed mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) over time, and 44% showed radiological progression. Notably, radiological and hormonal progression were largely independent—only 7.4% of patients with radiological progression also developed biochemical progression. Higher baseline 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test (DST) values predicted both biochemical progression and more substantial radiological growth (>10 mm). These findings highlight that current ESE/ENS@T guidelines, which lack specific BAI-tailored recommendations, may be insufficient for this subgroup.
items.caveat: Single-center retrospective design with modest sample size (120 enrolled, 61-64 completing full follow-up) limits generalizability; prospective multicenter studies are needed to define optimal surveillance intervals for BAIs specifically.
items.quiz_question: A 62-year-old woman with bilateral adrenal incidentalomas has a baseline 1-mg DST cortisol of 1.35 µg/dL (non-functioning by current criteria) and no radiological features of malignancy. Based on this cohort study, what is the approximate risk that she will develop MACS over a 3-year follow-up, and what baseline parameter best predicts this transition?
items.quiz_answer: Approximately 32% of initially non-functioning BAI patients developed MACS during follow-up. Higher baseline 1-mg DST cortisol values (even within the 'non-functioning' range) were the only parameter that significantly predicted biochemical progression, underscoring the importance of retesting cortisol autonomy over time in BAI patients.

items.title: MRI-based radiomics prediction of somatostatin receptor ligand response in acromegaly: an automated pipeline study.
items.summary: This multicenter study developed a fully automated MRI-based radiomics pipeline—incorporating tumor detection (YOLOv8), 3D segmentation, and machine-learning classification—to predict somatostatin receptor ligand (SRL) response in 49 acromegaly patients. The best-performing model, a 3-feature logistic regression using contrast-enhanced T1-weighted features, achieved an out-of-fold AUC of 0.798 and correctly classified 79.6% of patients. The most consistently discriminative feature was a gray-level co-occurrence matrix texture feature (ClusterShade), appearing in 98% of cross-validation folds. This represents a promising step toward non-invasive, pre-treatment prediction of SRL response to guide therapy selection.
items.caveat: The treatment-response cohort is small (n=49), and the pipeline was not externally validated in an independent acromegaly-specific dataset; results should be considered hypothesis-generating until prospective validation in larger multicenter cohorts is completed.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old man with newly diagnosed acromegaly secondary to a macroadenoma is being considered for primary medical therapy with a somatostatin receptor ligand versus upfront surgery. According to this radiomics study, what imaging modality and analytical approach showed the best performance for predicting SRL response, and what was the reported AUC?
items.quiz_answer: Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI features, analyzed via an automated radiomics pipeline with a 3-feature logistic regression classifier, achieved the best discriminative performance with an out-of-fold AUC of 0.798 (95% CI: 0.671–0.918), correctly classifying ~80% of patients as SRL responders or non-responders.

items.title: Osteoporosis and Skeletal Fragility in non-Metastatic Pheochromocytomas and Paragangliomas: The Adrenergic-Skeletal Axis.
items.summary: This review synthesizes emerging evidence that chronic catecholamine excess in pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma (PPGL) causes clinically significant skeletal harm—including increased bone turnover, reduced bone mineral density, impaired trabecular quality, and higher vertebral fracture prevalence—mediated through sympathetic innervation of bone and adrenergic receptor signaling on osteoblasts and osteoclasts. The review also raises the hypothesis that specific genetic backgrounds (VHL and SDHx mutations) may further modulate skeletal phenotype, independent of catecholamine secretion. The authors advocate for routine bone health screening in PPGL patients, a practice not yet standard in most centers.
items.caveat: The available clinical dataset is limited to a small number of studies with heterogeneous designs; the proposed role of VHL/SDHx mutations as skeletal phenotype modulators is described as speculative and requires prospective validation. This is a narrative review and does not provide new primary data.
items.quiz_question: A 45-year-old woman with a biochemically active, non-metastatic pheochromocytoma is referred for preoperative evaluation. She has no known risk factors for osteoporosis and is premenopausal. Should bone health assessment be part of her workup, and what is the pathophysiological rationale according to the adrenergic-skeletal axis concept?
items.quiz_answer: Yes—emerging evidence supports bone health screening in PPGL patients regardless of classic osteoporosis risk factors. Catecholamine excess activates β-adrenergic receptors on osteoblasts (suppressing bone formation) and promotes osteoclast activity, resulting in increased bone turnover and reduced BMD. Clinical studies have documented higher vertebral fracture prevalence in PPGL patients. DXA and vertebral fracture assessment should be considered, particularly in patients with long-standing or high catecholamine burden.

items.title: Clinical course and management of adrenal endocrine hypertension: A single-center experience.
items.summary: This retrospective single-center study of 55 patients with adrenal causes of secondary hypertension (PA 52.8%, PHEO 29.1%, ACTH-independent Cushing's 18.1%) found notably low rates of complete hypertension remission after definitive treatment: only 21.8% after adrenalectomy for PA, 37.5% for PHEO, and 40% for Cushing's. Patients with PA were diagnosed youngest and had the most severe, resistant hypertension requiring the most antihypertensive agents. PHEO patients were oldest at diagnosis and had more paroxysmal, severe hypertension, while CS patients had the least severe hypertensive phenotype and least end-organ damage. The data reinforce that adrenal endocrine hypertension carries significant residual cardiovascular risk even after cure, underscoring the importance of continued antihypertensive management post-operatively.
items.caveat: Small single-center retrospective cohort (n=55) with significant heterogeneity across three distinct adrenal etiologies; limited statistical power for subgroup comparisons, and no long-term cardiovascular outcome data beyond HTN remission rates.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old woman with primary aldosteronism undergoes successful unilateral adrenalectomy with confirmed biochemical cure (normalized aldosterone-renin ratio). Her preoperative blood pressure required three antihypertensive agents. Based on the best available evidence, what is the most realistic expectation regarding her hypertension after surgery?
items.quiz_answer: Complete hypertension remission occurs in only roughly 22% of surgically treated PA patients; most will still require antihypertensive therapy postoperatively, though the number of agents and BP control typically improve. Patients and clinicians should be counseled that biochemical cure does not equate to hypertension cure, and ongoing BP management remains essential.

items.title: Effectiveness of transsphenoidal surgery on remission and recurrence rates of pituitary adenomas: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 42 studies (6,416 patients, 2010–2025) found that endoscopic TSS (ETSS) achieved significantly higher endocrine remission rates than microscopic TSS (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.12–1.40), with descriptively lower recurrence rates (7.1% vs. 11.8%), though no direct comparative studies addressed recurrence as a primary endpoint. Gross total resection rates did not differ significantly between approaches. Visual remission following ETSS was reported in 81.8% of patients with optic chiasm compression, supporting its role as the preferred surgical modality for most PitNETs.
items.caveat: Recurrence comparisons are descriptive only—no direct head-to-head RCTs were available for this outcome. Significant heterogeneity exists across included studies in tumor types, surgeon experience, and remission criteria; the predominantly retrospective cohort design limits causal inference.
items.quiz_question: A 45-year-old man with Cushing's disease is being counseled on surgical options. His neurosurgeon is experienced in both microscopic and endoscopic transsphenoidal approaches. Based on current meta-analytic evidence, what advantage does the endoscopic approach confer regarding endocrine remission?
items.quiz_answer: The meta-analysis demonstrated a significantly higher endocrine remission rate with ETSS versus microscopic TSS (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.12–1.40), with descriptively lower recurrence rates (7.1% vs. 11.8%). For a patient with functioning PitNET such as Cushing's disease, endoscopic approach appears to offer a meaningful advantage in achieving hormonal remission, making it the preferred approach when expertise is available.

items.title: Prescription pattern of oral hydrocortisone by Indian healthcare professionals: An online questionnaire-based survey.
items.summary: This survey of 300 Indian healthcare professionals (84% response rate) found that oral hydrocortisone is widely and frequently prescribed for primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency and CAH, with high awareness of approved indications and tapering protocols. However, hyperglycemia and weight gain were the most frequently reported adverse effects (each ~43%), and nearly 90% of respondents expressed a desire for sustained-release hydrocortisone formulations—particularly for primary adrenal insufficiency—reflecting a recognized unmet clinical need that mirrors findings from Western practice surveys. Prednisolone was the most common alternative when hydrocortisone was not used.
items.caveat: Online survey methodology is subject to selection bias toward more engaged or specialist clinicians; the sample may not be representative of all Indian prescribers. Responses are self-reported and not validated against actual prescribing records.
items.quiz_question: A patient with primary adrenal insufficiency on conventional thrice-daily oral hydrocortisone reports persistent fatigue, particularly in the morning, and her HbA1c has risen. She asks whether there is a better formulation. What does current evidence and clinician survey data suggest about the unmet need here?
items.quiz_answer: Conventional immediate-release hydrocortisone has an unphysiological pharmacokinetic profile and is associated with metabolic adverse effects including hyperglycemia and weight gain. Survey data confirm that ~90% of clinicians recognize the need for modified-release formulations. Once-daily modified-release hydrocortisone (e.g., Plenadren) better mimics the physiological cortisol rhythm and has been associated with improved metabolic profiles in clinical trials, making it a clinically reasonable option to discuss in this patient.

items.title: Dietary Interventions and Vitamin D3 Replacement in Pituitary Tumors: a Systematic Review.
items.summary: This systematic review of 8 studies (355 participants) examined dietary strategies across acromegaly, Cushing's disease, prolactinoma, and hypopituitarism. Very low-carbohydrate ketogenic diets reduced IGF-I in acromegaly and improved BMI/metabolic parameters in Cushing's disease, while energy-restricted diets combined with physical activity benefited prolactinoma and hypopituitarism patients. Vitamin D3 replacement was associated with reduced vertebral fracture risk in acromegaly and improved insulin sensitivity and lipid profiles in Cushing's disease, suggesting adjunctive dietary and nutritional strategies deserve a formal place in PitNET management discussions.
items.caveat: Only 8 small heterogeneous studies met inclusion criteria; most are observational or have high risk of bias, and the evidence base is insufficient to support formal dietary prescriptions without larger randomized trials.
items.quiz_question: A 45-year-old woman with active Cushing's disease awaiting surgery asks about lifestyle modifications that might help her metabolic comorbidities in the interim. Based on the best available (though limited) evidence, which dietary approach and nutritional supplement have shown the most promise for improving BMI/metabolic parameters and insulin sensitivity, respectively?
items.quiz_answer: Very low-carbohydrate ketogenic or energy-restricted diets have shown improvement in BMI and metabolic parameters in Cushing's disease, while vitamin D3 replacement was associated with improved insulin sensitivity and lipid levels in this population, per this systematic review. Both should be considered adjuncts, not replacements for definitive therapy, given the limited evidence base.

items.title: Endoscopic endonasal approach for recurrent or residual pituitary neuroendocrine tumors.
items.summary: This retrospective series of 152 patients undergoing repeat endoscopic endonasal surgery (EES) for recurrent or residual PitNETs demonstrated a gross total resection (GTR) rate of 69.1%, with visual field improvement in 72.5% of those with preoperative deficits. The complication profile was acceptable: new permanent diabetes insipidus occurred in only 1.3% and new hypopituitarism in 7.9%. Critically, Knosp grade 3–4 was the strongest independent predictor of incomplete resection (OR >86), underscoring the importance of cavernous sinus involvement in surgical planning for redo cases.
items.caveat: Retrospective single-center design with patient selection bias (only those deemed suitable for repeat EES were included); the very high OR for Knosp 3–4 is imprecise due to sparse data in that subgroup. Median follow-up of 36 months may be insufficient to capture late recurrences.
items.quiz_question: A 52-year-old man with a non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma underwent transsphenoidal resection 3 years ago; MRI now shows a 2 cm residual tumor with Knosp grade 4 cavernous sinus invasion. He is referred for consideration of repeat EES. What does this large retrospective series suggest about his likelihood of achieving GTR, and what is the principal predictor of incomplete resection?
items.quiz_answer: Knosp grade 3–4 was the single strongest predictor of incomplete resection (OR >86) in this series, meaning patients like this one with Knosp 4 involvement have a substantially lower chance of achieving GTR. Overall GTR was 69.1% across the cohort, but this drops significantly for high Knosp-grade tumors, and alternative or adjunctive strategies (radiosurgery, medical therapy) should be part of the multidisciplinary discussion.

items.title: Intracranial germ cell tumors: an underrecognized diagnostic consideration in adults with sellar/suprasellar lesions.
items.summary: In a single-center study of 48 adults (≥18 years) with sellar/suprasellar intracranial germ cell tumors (iGCTs), the median age at onset was 23.4 years and 87.5% were male. CSF β-hCG distinguished iGCTs from lymphocytic hypophysitis (LYH) with an AUC of 0.897 at a cutoff of 2.52 U/L (sensitivity 78.6%, specificity 95.5%). A nomogram incorporating sex, log-transformed serum β-hCG, hyperprolactinemia, and pituitary stalk thickening further improved discrimination (AUC 0.939), offering a practical framework to avoid delayed diagnosis of this treatable condition in adults presenting with hypopituitarism and stalk lesions.
items.caveat: Single-center retrospective study with internal bootstrap validation only; external validation in independent cohorts is required before the nomogram can be broadly adopted. The LYH comparator group limits generalizability to the full differential of pituitary stalk lesions.
items.quiz_question: A 24-year-old male presents with diabetes insipidus, hyperprolactinemia, and a thickened pituitary stalk on MRI. Serum β-hCG is mildly elevated. You are considering lymphocytic hypophysitis versus an intracranial germ cell tumor. According to this study, what CSF marker and cutoff best differentiates these two entities, and what other clinical features favor iGCT?
items.quiz_answer: CSF β-hCG >2.52 U/L had a sensitivity of 78.6% and specificity of 95.5% for distinguishing iGCT from LYH (AUC 0.897). Male sex, elevated serum β-hCG, hyperprolactinemia, and pituitary stalk thickening together (incorporated in the nomogram) further favor iGCT. Young male patients with these features warrant CSF analysis and oncologic workup before attributing stalk lesions to autoimmune hypophysitis.

items.title: Adrenal insufficiency in individuals with Duchenne muscular dystrophy treated with glucocorticoids: Insights from the past, current challenges, and future directions.
items.summary: This review provides updated best-practice guidance on managing iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency (AI) in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) patients on chronic high-dose glucocorticoids — a group at particularly high risk given prolonged supraphysiologic GC exposure from a young age. Key themes include caregiver/patient education on adrenal suppression recognition, stress-dosing protocols, safe transitions between GC regimens (e.g., deflazacort to prednisone or vice versa), and strategies for safe GC discontinuation. The review also notes applicability to Becker muscular dystrophy and female manifesting carriers on individualized GC regimens.
items.caveat: This is a narrative review without a formal systematic methodology; recommendations are consensus/expert-based and may not be uniformly evidence-graded. The DMD therapeutic landscape is rapidly evolving (gene therapy, exon skipping), and GC tapering guidance may need updating as these agents displace or modify GC use.
items.quiz_question: A 14-year-old male with DMD on deflazacort 0.9 mg/kg/day for 8 years is transitioning to a reduced-dose regimen due to side effects. He presents to the ED with vomiting and fatigue after a GI illness. His parents report he missed two doses. What is the most important immediate management consideration?
items.quiz_answer: This patient is at high risk for acute adrenal insufficiency given prolonged supraphysiologic GC exposure causing HPA axis suppression. He should receive empiric stress-dose hydrocortisone (e.g., 50–100 mg/m² IV bolus, then divided doses over 24 hours) without waiting for confirmatory cortisol levels, as per AI stress-dosing protocols outlined for DMD patients in this review.

items.title: Clinically silent pheochromocytoma presenting as an adrenal incidentaloma: the importance of biochemical evaluation.
items.summary: This case report describes a woman in her late 70s with a 5 cm left adrenal incidentaloma discovered incidentally, who had long-standing well-controlled hypertension and no classic catecholamine-excess symptoms — yet biochemical evaluation revealed elevated plasma free metanephrines confirming pheochromocytoma. CT showed a predominantly cystic lesion with elevated unenhanced attenuation values atypical for adenoma. Minimally invasive resection achieved biochemical cure, reinforcing that clinical silence does not exclude functionally active pheochromocytoma and that biochemical screening is obligatory for all adrenal incidentalomas regardless of symptom status.
items.caveat: Single case report; provides illustrative rather than epidemiologic evidence. The reminder about mandatory biochemical testing is guideline-concordant (Endocrine Society 2023 adrenal incidentaloma guidelines), so the clinical lesson is not novel — but the case usefully reinforces the point for elderly patients without classic adrenergic features.
items.quiz_question: A 78-year-old woman with a history of treated hypertension undergoes abdominal CT for diverticulitis workup, revealing a 5.2 cm left adrenal mass with an unenhanced HU of 28. She denies headaches, palpitations, or sweating. Her blood pressure is 138/82 mmHg on two antihypertensives. What is the next required step in evaluation?
items.quiz_answer: Biochemical testing for pheochromocytoma — specifically plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urine fractionated metanephrines — is mandatory regardless of the absence of classic adrenergic symptoms, as this case demonstrates that clinically silent pheochromocytoma can present as an adrenal incidentaloma. Elevated unenhanced attenuation (>10 HU) is also atypical for a benign adenoma and further mandates functional workup before any biopsy or intervention.

items.title: Pituitary adenomas in older patients - approaches, challenges and future directions.
items.summary: This review synthesizes 20 years of published data on pituitary adenomas diagnosed in elderly patients, highlighting that clinical phenotypes often differ substantially from younger cohorts — for example, acromegaly and prolactinoma may present atypically, and age-related pituitary changes can confound hormonal interpretation. Diagnosis is complicated by overlap between normal aging (e.g., declining IGF-1, declining gonadotropins, visual changes) and adenoma-related findings. The authors emphasize individualized, patient-tailored management that accounts for frailty, polypharmacy, and patient preferences, and advocate for management at centers of excellence with multidisciplinary expertise.
items.caveat: Narrative review with a 20-year literature window, which includes heterogeneous study designs and populations; no meta-analytic pooling. Specific evidence for outcomes in elderly patients with pituitary adenomas remains sparse compared to younger populations, limiting the strength of age-specific recommendations.
items.quiz_question: A 78-year-old man is referred for a newly diagnosed 2.2 cm non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma found incidentally on MRI. He is frail with mild cognitive impairment, stable visual fields, and no hormonal excess. His family asks about surgery. How should his management differ from that of a 45-year-old with the same finding?
items.quiz_answer: In elderly and/or frail patients with incidental non-functioning pituitary macroadenomas and preserved visual fields, a conservative watchful-waiting approach is generally preferred over upfront surgery, as surgical risk is amplified by frailty, comorbidities, and reduced physiologic reserve. Management should be individualized with input from a multidisciplinary pituitary team, weighing the patient's wishes, functional status, and life expectancy — rather than applying the same intervention thresholds used for younger, surgically fit patients.

items.title: Pituitary Society Delphi consensus on the role of radiotherapy for pituitary adenomas.
items.summary: A modified two-round Delphi panel of 29 international experts (neuroendocrinologists, neurosurgeons, radiation oncologists) reached consensus on 24 of 27 statements regarding radiotherapy for pituitary adenomas. Key agreements include: radiotherapy indication and technique should be decided by expert multidisciplinary tumor boards including a radiation oncologist; hormonal hypersecretion should be controlled medically while awaiting radiotherapy's delayed efficacy in functioning adenomas; and long-term follow-up exceeding 10 years is required to assess delayed efficacy, recurrence, and side effects. Modern radiotherapy techniques were judged effective and potentially safer than prior approaches, with a recognized shift from fractionated radiotherapy toward stereotactic radiosurgery in appropriately selected patients.
items.caveat: Delphi consensus reflects expert opinion rather than randomized trial data; panelists acknowledged that further long-term comparative outcome data are still needed, and practice variation across institutions and healthcare systems may limit generalizability.
items.quiz_question: A 55-year-old patient with a residual GH-secreting macroadenoma after transsphenoidal surgery has persistently elevated IGF-1 despite maximum-dose octreotide LAR. The multidisciplinary tumor board is considering stereotactic radiosurgery. According to the Pituitary Society Delphi consensus, what is the recommended approach to managing hormonal excess during the period between radiosurgery delivery and expected onset of its biochemical effect?
items.quiz_answer: The consensus recommends continuing medical therapy to control hormonal hypersecretion while awaiting the delayed efficacy of radiotherapy, as the biochemical effect of radiosurgery typically unfolds over months to years. The panel emphasized this as a key management principle for functioning adenomas undergoing radiotherapy.

items.title: Pasireotide-LAR and pegvisomant combination in resistant acromegaly: a case series of predominantly mammosomatotroph adenomas.
items.summary: This single-center retrospective case series reports outcomes in six patients (predominantly mammosomatotroph adenomas, ages 15–44) with treatment-resistant acromegaly who received combination pasireotide-LAR plus pegvisomant over a median of 3.3 years after failing surgery and multiple prior medical therapies. All six achieved normal IGF-1 and tumor stability, though one required additional surgery and radiosurgery after biochemical escape at 9 months. Importantly, three of six developed hyperglycemia in the pre-diabetes range, and concurrent pegvisomant use did not appear to mitigate pasireotide-induced glycemic deterioration—underscoring the need for proactive glucose monitoring in this combination.
items.caveat: Extremely small sample size (n=6) from a single tertiary center limits generalizability; retrospective design precludes causal conclusions; the predominantly mammosomatotroph histology may not represent the broader acromegaly population; no comparator arm.
items.quiz_question: A 28-year-old woman with a mammosomatotroph macroadenoma has persistently elevated IGF-1 despite transsphenoidal surgery and sequential trials of octreotide LAR and cabergoline. You initiate pasireotide-LAR 40 mg every 28 days and plan to add pegvisomant. What metabolic parameter requires close monitoring, and does adding pegvisomant reliably protect against this complication?
items.quiz_answer: Blood glucose (and HbA1c) must be monitored closely, as pasireotide-LAR causes hyperglycemia via inhibition of insulin secretion. Based on this case series, co-administration of pegvisomant does not appear to mitigate pasireotide-induced glycemic deterioration—three of six patients developed pre-diabetes range hyperglycemia despite combination therapy.

items.title: Distinguishing hyperparathyroidism from insulin-like growth factor I-driven calcium-phosphate metabolism changes in acromegaly.
items.summary: In a retrospective study of 393 patients with acromegaly at two French university hospitals, 5.9% had concomitant primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT). In patients with isolated acromegaly, mild hypercalcemia (3.2%) and hyperphosphatemia (37.3%) resolved after acromegaly treatment, whereas PHPT patients had persistent hypercalcemia with low-to-normal phosphate and elevated PTH. A simple threshold-based decision rule—calcium >2.60 mmol/L combined with phosphate <1.46 mmol/L—demonstrated excellent discriminatory performance (bootstrapped sensitivity 94%, specificity 99.3%) for identifying parathyroid autonomy, outperforming more complex machine learning models in interpretability while matching their accuracy.
items.caveat: Retrospective design with potential referral bias at two specialized centers; the diagnostic rule was developed and internally validated in the same cohort (bootstrap correction applied but no independent external validation); no pathogenic gene variants were found in tested genes, but not all MEN1-related genes were necessarily screened.
items.quiz_question: A 48-year-old man with active acromegaly (elevated IGF-1, unsuppressed GH) is found to have serum calcium 2.68 mmol/L and serum phosphate 0.85 mmol/L. PTH is mildly elevated. How should you interpret this biochemical picture, and what does this study suggest regarding further workup?
items.quiz_answer: The combination of calcium >2.60 mmol/L with a low-normal phosphate (<1.46 mmol/L) and elevated PTH points strongly toward concomitant primary hyperparathyroidism rather than IGF-1-driven mineral disturbance, which typically causes hyperphosphatemia and resolves with acromegaly treatment. This study's threshold-based rule (Ca >2.60 + PO4 <1.46) had 94% sensitivity and 99.3% specificity for PHPT in acromegaly, supporting dedicated parathyroid evaluation in this patient.

items.title: Dexamethasone Nonsuppression in Primary Aldosteronism: Associations With Adrenal Imaging Findings.
items.summary: In this prospective observational study of 883 hypertensive patients evaluated for primary aldosteronism (PA), 12.2% showed 1-mg DST nonsuppression (post-DST cortisol >1.8 µg/dL). Nonsuppression prevalence increased stepwise from non-PA patients to PA without adrenal nodules to PA with adrenal nodules, with adrenal nodules independently associated with DST nonsuppression (OR 2.68, 95% CI 1.01–7.12) after propensity score adjustment. Notably, even among PA patients without adrenal nodules on CT, DST nonsuppression correlated with lower eGFR and higher prevalence of chronic kidney disease, suggesting clinically meaningful autonomous cortisol co-secretion even when imaging is negative.
items.caveat: Single-center prospective observational design limits generalizability; causal direction between MACS and CKD cannot be established, and overt Cushing's syndrome was excluded by definition but subclinical hypercortisolism was not formally quantified beyond the DST cutoff.
items.quiz_question: A 55-year-old hypertensive man is confirmed to have primary aldosteronism. His CT shows no adrenal nodules. His 1-mg DST post-cortisol is 2.3 µg/dL. Based on this study's findings, what additional clinical concern does this DST result raise, and what is the association with renal function?
items.quiz_answer: Even in PA patients without adrenal nodules, DST nonsuppression (post-cortisol >1.8 µg/dL) was associated with lower estimated GFR and a higher prevalence of chronic kidney disease in this study, suggesting that mild autonomous cortisol co-secretion carries cardiometabolic consequences independent of visible adrenal nodules and should not be dismissed as spurious.
items.journal: Journal of the American Heart Association

items.title: The Functional Side of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1-Associated Adrenal Disease: Mild Autonomous Cortisol Secretion.
items.summary: This retrospective single-center study is the first to specifically characterize mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) in MEN1 patients with radiologically confirmed adrenal involvement. Among 22 MEN1 patients who underwent complete hormonal evaluation, MACS (post-1 mg DST cortisol >1.8 µg/dL without overt Cushing's) was identified in 15 (68.2%)—a strikingly higher prevalence than reported for sporadic adrenal incidentalomas. Patients with MACS had significantly lower baseline ACTH concentrations and a trend toward higher metabolic syndrome prevalence, suggesting that autonomous cortisol co-secretion may be an under-recognized contributor to cardiometabolic burden in MEN1.
items.caveat: Very small evaluated sample (n=22 with complete hormonal data out of 101 MEN1 patients), retrospective single-center design, and absence of a control group limit the strength of conclusions; prospective multicenter validation is clearly needed before routine screening recommendations can be formalized.
items.quiz_question: A 42-year-old woman with genetically confirmed MEN1 is found to have a 2.2 cm left adrenal adenoma on surveillance imaging. Her aldosterone, metanephrines, and androgens are all normal. Should you perform a 1-mg DST, and what prevalence of MACS does this study suggest in this population?
items.quiz_answer: Yes, a 1-mg DST is warranted. This study found MACS in 68.2% of MEN1 patients with adrenal involvement who underwent complete evaluation—substantially higher than in sporadic incidentalomas—making systematic cortisol autonomy screening a clinically important step in MEN1 adrenal management despite the preliminary nature of the data.

items.title: Management of ectopic Cushing syndrome in medullary thyroid carcinoma: from case reports to systematic literature review.
items.summary: This PRISMA-compliant systematic review compiled 99 published cases of ectopic Cushing's syndrome (ECS) due to medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), supplemented by four new institutional cases. Over half of patients presented with distant metastases at diagnosis, and hypercortisolism was frequently refractory to medical therapy—requiring bilateral adrenalectomy as rescue in 33 patients. Importantly, emerging data on selective RET inhibitors (particularly selpercatinib) showed rapid biochemical improvement and radiologic responses in all five reported cases where they were used, suggesting simultaneous tumor and cortisol control may be achievable in RET-mutated disease.
items.caveat: The systematic review is entirely case-report–level evidence with substantial heterogeneity in reporting, and the selpercatinib data comprise only five cases—far too few to establish efficacy or guide treatment sequencing. Publication bias likely overrepresents dramatic or treatment-responsive cases.
items.quiz_question: A 52-year-old man with metastatic sporadic MTC (somatic RET M918T mutation) develops severe hypokalemia, proximal myopathy, and uncontrolled hyperglycemia. ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism is confirmed, with inferior petrosal sinus sampling ruling out a pituitary source. Medical management of hypercortisolism has failed. What does this systematic review suggest as both a potential rescue strategy for hypercortisolism and a disease-directed therapy?
items.quiz_answer: Bilateral adrenalectomy was used as rescue therapy in 33 patients in this review when medical management failed. Additionally, the review highlights emerging evidence that selpercatinib (a selective RET inhibitor) may simultaneously control tumor progression and cortisol excess in RET-mutated MTC, with rapid biochemical responses reported in all five cases described—though current data remain limited to case reports.

items.title: Clinical characteristics and prognostic outcomes of silent corticotroph versus gonadotroph adenomas: A 603-case single-center cohort study.
items.summary: In this large single-center cohort of 603 non-functioning pituitary adenomas, silent corticotroph adenomas (SCAs) were more common in younger women and displayed more aggressive behavior than silent gonadotroph adenomas (SGAs): larger tumor size, higher rates of cavernous sinus invasion (69% vs. 41%), more intratumoral hemorrhage, lower gross total resection rates, and notably higher postoperative venous thromboembolism risk (16% vs. 9.6%). Recurrence predictors differed meaningfully between subtypes—younger age, subtotal resection, and firm consistency drove SCA recurrence, while tumor size, Ki-67 ≥3%, and firm consistency predicted SGA recurrence. Nomograms for 2- and 4-year radiological progression showed strong internal discriminative ability (AUCs 0.93/0.91 for SCAs; 0.90/0.88 for SGAs), supporting individualized surveillance planning.
items.caveat: Retrospective single-center design from one Chinese institution limits generalizability; nomograms require external validation before clinical adoption, and immunohistochemical subtyping methodology details are not fully elaborated in the abstract.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old woman undergoes transsphenoidal resection of a non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma. Pathology returns as a silent corticotroph adenoma with subtotal resection due to cavernous sinus invasion. Based on this study's findings, which additional postoperative complication should be specifically anticipated at a higher rate compared to silent gonadotroph adenoma patients?
items.quiz_answer: Venous thromboembolism (VTE). SCAs had a significantly higher rate of postoperative VTE (16% vs. 9.6% in SGAs, P=0.025), making prophylaxis and vigilance particularly important in this subtype.

items.title: A structured approach to address variability in the global management of adrenal insufficiency in Duchenne muscular dystrophy: the 2025 PJ Nicholoff steroid protocol.
items.summary: This review addresses the increasingly complex challenge of managing glucocorticoid-induced adrenal suppression in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), where patients may receive prednisone/prednisolone, deflazacort, or the newer agent vamorolone on daily or intermittent schedules. The updated 2025 PJ Nicholoff Steroid Protocol provides a DMD-specific practical framework covering anticipatory education, written weight-based stress-dose steroid plans, safe tapering algorithms, confirmation of HPA axis recovery, and structured guidance for transitions between GC agents—including vamorolone, for which stress-dosing experience is still limited. The authors highlight that global variability in drug availability, institutional protocols, and caregiver education creates meaningful safety gaps for a population at high risk for adrenal crisis during illness or surgical stress.
items.caveat: This is a consensus/expert framework review rather than a prospective clinical trial; evidence for vamorolone-specific HPA suppression and optimal stress-dosing thresholds remains limited, and the protocol has not yet been validated in outcome studies.
items.quiz_question: A 12-year-old boy with Duchenne muscular dystrophy on daily deflazacort develops a febrile respiratory illness and his parents are unsure whether to give stress-dose steroids. According to the principles outlined in the 2025 PJ Nicholoff Protocol, what key elements should his written stress-steroid plan include to guide his caregivers in this situation?
items.quiz_answer: The plan should include a weight-based stress-dose calculation (typically 3× the physiologic replacement equivalent), clear triggers for when to administer it (fever, vomiting, significant physiological stress, missed doses), instructions on route escalation if the child cannot take oral medication, and guidance on when to seek emergency care—all part of anticipatory caregiver education emphasized by the protocol.

items.title: An interpretable machine learning framework using multi-phase computed tomography for differentiation of adrenal lipid-poor adenomas and pheochromocytomas.
items.summary: This retrospective study of 229 pathologically confirmed adrenal tumors (132 lipid-poor adenomas, 97 pheochromocytomas) developed an interpretable decision-tree (DT) machine learning model using multi-phase CT radiomic features to distinguish these two entities, which can be challenging when standard lipid-rich criteria are absent. The DT model achieved excellent AUCs of 0.977 (washout cohort) and 0.983 (non-washout cohort), with cystic degeneration identified as the most influential discriminator, followed by enhancement potential and baseline attenuation. The inherently transparent decision logic of the DT approach offers a clinically actionable advantage over black-box models, potentially supporting radiologists in managing indeterminate adrenal lesions without requiring biopsy.
items.caveat: Retrospective single-institution design with a relatively small sample (n=229); the model has not been externally validated, and the high AUCs likely reflect optimistic performance that may not reproduce across imaging platforms or clinical settings. Biochemical exclusion of pheochromocytoma before any invasive workup remains mandatory regardless of imaging model output.
items.quiz_question: A 55-year-old man has a 3.2 cm adrenal mass with non-contrast attenuation of 25 HU (lipid-poor). Multi-phase CT shows no cystic degeneration and moderate enhancement with an absolute percentage washout of 45% (non-washout criteria). According to this study's decision-tree model, which CT feature is the single most important discriminator between lipid-poor adenoma and pheochromocytoma, and what is its significance in this case?
items.quiz_answer: Cystic degeneration was identified as the most influential discriminator in the model. Its absence in this case slightly favors adenoma, but enhancement potential and baseline attenuation are the next key variables in the decision tree. Critically, biochemical testing for catecholamine excess must be performed before any biopsy or invasive procedure regardless of imaging findings.

items.title: The value of the modified Knosp grade in pituitary adenoma surgery.
items.summary: In a prospectively collected single-center cohort of 482 patients undergoing pure endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery, the modified Knosp grade was the strongest independent predictor of gross total resection (GTR). GTR rates ranged from 97% at grade 0 to just 7% at grade 4, with the 3A/3B subdivision proving particularly informative: grade 3B carried significantly higher rates of incomplete resection than 3A. These findings provide robust external validation of the modified Knosp grading system across a large contemporary cohort.
items.caveat: Single-institution retrospective-prospective hybrid study spanning 2011–2024; interrater reliability of the modified Knosp grading is acknowledged as a limitation for interinstitutional reproducibility, though that was explicitly the aim of validation.
items.quiz_question: A 45-year-old man with acromegaly has a macroadenoma encasing the internal carotid artery and extending beyond the lateral tangent of the cavernous sinus on both sides, meeting modified Knosp grade 3B criteria on MRI. How should this grading influence your preoperative counseling regarding surgical cure?
items.quiz_answer: Modified Knosp grade 3B is associated with a significantly lower GTR rate compared to grade 3A (35% vs 45% overall in this cohort), and is the strongest independent predictor of incomplete resection. The patient and referring neurosurgeon should be counseled that biochemical remission from surgery alone is unlikely, and multimodal planning—including adjuvant somatostatin receptor ligand therapy or stereotactic radiosurgery—should be discussed preoperatively.
