items.title: Prevalence and Predictors of Remission in Patients with Acromegaly Undergoing Microscopic or Endoscopic Transsphenoidal Surgery: Long-Term Outcomes from a Tertiary Care Centre.
items.summary: In this retrospective single-center series of 169 acromegaly patients followed for a mean of 5.2 years after transsphenoidal surgery, only 31.3% achieved endocrine remission by 2014 consensus criteria (random GH <1 µg/L and age-normalized IGF-1). Baseline tumor size and pretreatment nadir GH were the only independent predictors of both remission and need for adjuvant therapy, while baseline GH alone predicted disease activity at last follow-up. Adjuvant therapy was ultimately required in 46% of the cohort, underscoring the high rate of surgical non-cure even at a dedicated center.
items.caveat: Retrospective single-center design from a tertiary referral center in India; mean diagnostic delay of ~5 years suggests a more advanced disease population at presentation, which may limit generalizability to centers with earlier detection. Mixed microscopic and endoscopic cases could introduce surgical heterogeneity.
items.quiz_question: A 40-year-old woman presents with acromegaly. Her preoperative IGF-1 is 3× ULN, random GH is 22 µg/L, and MRI shows a 2.8 cm macroadenoma with modified Knosp grade 2 cavernous sinus involvement. Based on findings from this study, what preoperative factors best predict her likelihood of achieving remission, and what should she be told about the probability of needing adjuvant therapy?
items.quiz_answer: Baseline tumor size and pretreatment nadir GH were the strongest independent predictors of remission and adjuvant therapy need. A large macroadenoma with elevated nadir GH portends a lower chance of surgical cure; in this cohort overall remission was only 31.3%. She should be counseled that adjuvant therapy (somatostatin receptor ligands, pegvisomant, or radiosurgery) is statistically more likely than not, and treatment planning should incorporate this expectation from the outset.
items.journal: Indian journal of endocrinology and metabolism

items.title: Beyond insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) normalization: portal insulin and hepatic growth hormone (GH) sensitivity across metabolic disease.
items.summary: This review proposes 'liver sensitivity to GH' (LSG)—operationally defined by portal-insulin-determined hepatic GH receptor availability—as a unifying mechanistic framework linking GH deficiency, acromegaly, obesity, type 1 and 2 diabetes, and cirrhosis on a single continuum. The authors argue that subcutaneous insulin in T1D corrects glycemia but leaves hepatic GH resistance intact due to the absence of physiologic portal insulin delivery, explaining persistent low IGF-1 despite systemic euglycemia. They also re-examine why GLP-1 receptor agonists produce discordant GH/IGF-1 signatures and argue that current acromegaly treatment targets (IGF-1 normalization alone) may be metabolically insufficient when viewed through this portal-insulin lens.
items.caveat: This is a mechanistic review/opinion piece without original clinical trial data; the LSG framework is hypothesis-generating and not yet validated prospectively. The proposed clinical implications for acromegaly management targets await empirical testing.
items.quiz_question: A 28-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes and GH deficiency receives subcutaneous insulin and GH replacement. Despite apparently adequate GH dosing, her IGF-1 remains persistently below normal. Using the portal-insulin/LSG framework described in this review, what is the most likely mechanistic explanation?
items.quiz_answer: Subcutaneous insulin delivery bypasses the portal vein, resulting in peripheral hyperinsulinism relative to portal delivery. Hepatic GH receptor expression and signaling depend on adequate portal insulin concentration; without physiologic portal insulinization, hepatic GH sensitivity (LSG) remains impaired, so exogenous GH fails to generate normal IGF-1 output despite systemic insulin adequacy. This is distinct from true GH dose insufficiency.

items.title: Hypothalamic obesity in pediatric vs. adult craniopharyngioma: mechanisms, management, and cardiometabolic outcomes.
items.summary: This scoping review systematically compares hypothalamic obesity (HO) in pediatric versus adult craniopharyngioma survivors, finding a far steeper post-treatment obesity rise in children (5.7% → 57%) than adults (19.2% → 29.2%). Key shared mechanisms include disrupted melanocortin signaling and central leptin/insulin resistance, with neuroinflammatory pathways (resistin-TLR4, NLRP3) also implicated. GLP-1 receptor agonists showed promising weight loss in small case series (up to 17% over 6 months with semaglutide), though randomized trials did not meet their primary weight endpoints. Long-term cardiometabolic burden is substantial in both cohorts, with adults carrying a 2.2-fold higher all-cause mortality and 9.3-fold higher diabetes risk.
items.caveat: Scoping review design limits causal inference; head-to-head pediatric vs. adult therapeutic trials are lacking, and GLP-1 agonist data derive from small, uncontrolled case series only.
items.quiz_question: A 10-year-old boy undergoes gross-total resection of a craniopharyngioma with significant hypothalamic involvement. His parents ask about long-term weight risk. Based on current evidence, approximately what proportion of pediatric craniopharyngioma survivors develop obesity post-treatment, and what mechanism primarily drives it?
items.quiz_answer: Approximately 57% of pediatric craniopharyngioma survivors develop obesity post-treatment (up from ~6% pre-treatment). The primary driver is hypothalamic damage disrupting melanocortin signaling and inducing central leptin and insulin resistance, leading to hyperphagia and profoundly reduced energy expenditure — the hallmarks of hypothalamic obesity.

items.title: Adrenal Tumors Identified on Abdominal Imaging in Breast Cancer Patients: Benign Incidentalomas or Metastatic Disease?
items.summary: In this single-institution review of 2,745 breast cancer patients, 3.8% had adrenal tumors detected on abdominal imaging; 77% were benign, 11% metastatic, and 13% indeterminate. Multivariate analysis identified three independent predictors of adrenal metastasis: presence of other metastatic sites on the same scan (OR 7.73), larger initial tumor size (OR 1.90 per cm), and detection on a surveillance scan (OR 8.60). Mean tumor size was significantly larger in metastases (2.4 vs. 1.7 cm), though there was considerable overlap. These findings provide a practical risk-stratification framework for deciding when to pursue biopsy in breast cancer patients with adrenal lesions.
items.caveat: Single-institution retrospective study with a relatively small number of confirmed metastases (n=11), limiting statistical power; radiologic criteria for classification were predetermined but may not align with all institutional protocols. Functional adrenal evaluation details are not described.
items.quiz_question: A 58-year-old woman with stage IV breast cancer (known bone metastases) is found to have a new 2.8 cm right adrenal mass on surveillance CT. The lesion has an unenhanced HU of 18. What clinical and imaging features most strongly predict this represents metastatic rather than benign disease, and what is the appropriate next step?
items.quiz_answer: The strongest independent predictors of adrenal metastasis in breast cancer patients are: concurrent other metastatic sites (OR 7.73), larger tumor size (OR 1.90/cm), and detection on surveillance imaging (OR 8.60). This patient has all three risk factors. The indeterminate Hounsfield unit (18 HU) rules out a lipid-rich adenoma. Given high metastatic probability, percutaneous biopsy (after biochemical exclusion of pheochromocytoma) is appropriate to confirm diagnosis and guide systemic therapy.

items.title: Growth hormone-releasing hormone, growth hormone, and neuroendocrine tumors.
items.summary: This review summarizes the clinical presentation and diagnostic challenges of ectopic acromegaly due to GHRH- or GH-secreting neuroendocrine tumors (NETs), which are rare but frequently misdiagnosed as pituitary-origin acromegaly because clinical features are indistinguishable. Serum GHRH measurement is highlighted as a critical diagnostic tool when ectopic production is suspected — particularly when pituitary imaging is non-confirmatory or when somatostatin analog response is atypical. Surgical resection of the offending NET remains first-line therapy; somatostatin receptor analogs and chemo/immunotherapy serve as adjuncts in refractory cases. Advanced molecular imaging is increasingly important in localizing the ectopic source.
items.caveat: Evidence base is limited by extreme rarity of these tumors; no prospective trials exist, and recommendations derive largely from case series and expert opinion. Comprehensive guidelines are explicitly noted as lacking.
items.quiz_question: A 45-year-old woman presents with classic acromegalic features: acral enlargement, prognathism, and elevated IGF-1. Pituitary MRI shows only a 4 mm questionable microadenoma. She has a known pulmonary carcinoid on prior imaging. What diagnostic step should be prioritized to distinguish ectopic from pituitary-origin acromegaly, and what does the treatment algorithm look like if ectopic GHRH secretion is confirmed?
items.quiz_answer: Serum GHRH measurement should be prioritized — an elevated level strongly supports ectopic GHRH secretion rather than a primary GH-secreting pituitary adenoma. If elevated, advanced functional imaging (e.g., somatostatin receptor scintigraphy or DOTATATE PET-CT) should localize the NET. First-line treatment is surgical resection of the offending carcinoid; somatostatin receptor analogs can control GH/IGF-1 hypersecretion pre- or post-operatively, with chemo/immunotherapy reserved for refractory disease.

items.title: Mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) is associated with increased mortality in patients with adrenal adenomas only in the presence of type 2 diabetes: a retrospective cohort study.
items.summary: In this retrospective cohort of 668 patients with adrenal adenomas followed over two decades at a single tertiary center, MACS (post-1 mg DST cortisol >1.8 µg/dL) was associated with a significantly increased mortality hazard only in those who also carried a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes (HR 2.51, 95% CI 1.41–4.48), but not in patients without T2D. The T2D+MACS subgroup had higher HbA1c and a three-fold elevation in prevalent cardiovascular disease compared to T2D patients with non-functioning adenomas. These data suggest that T2D may act as an effect modifier that unmasks the lethal cardiometabolic consequences of even mild cortisol excess, and argue for heightened vigilance—and potentially earlier intervention—in this overlap population.
items.caveat: Retrospective single-center design with inherent selection bias; causality cannot be established, and residual confounding from diabetes severity, duration, and medications is possible. Sample sizes in subgroups are modest, and the authors themselves call for confirmatory prospective studies.
items.quiz_question: A 62-year-old woman with long-standing type 2 diabetes is found to have a 2.3 cm left adrenal adenoma. Her post-1 mg DST cortisol is 2.4 µg/dL without overt Cushing's stigmata, meeting criteria for MACS. She has well-controlled hypertension and dyslipidemia. Based on this study's findings, how should her MACS status influence your management approach compared to a similar patient without T2D?
items.quiz_answer: This study found that MACS was associated with a >2.5-fold increased mortality specifically in patients with T2D, but not in those without T2D. Accordingly, her concurrent T2D substantially elevates the clinical significance of the MACS diagnosis, warranting more active cardiometabolic risk reduction, closer follow-up, and serious consideration of adrenalectomy if she is a surgical candidate—a conversation that might be deferred in an otherwise identical patient without diabetes.

items.title: The cardiometabolic significance of post-dexamethasone cortisol levels below the MACS threshold in adrenal incidentaloma.
items.summary: This retrospective cross-sectional study of 156 patients with adrenal incidentalomas stratified by post-1 mg DST cortisol into three tiers (≤0.9, 0.91–1.79, and ≥1.8 µg/dL) found a graded cardiometabolic risk pattern across all groups. Importantly, patients in the intermediate 'below-MACS-threshold' group (0.91–1.79 µg/dL) already showed significantly higher blood pressure, hypertension prevalence, HbA1c, and LDL cholesterol compared to those with complete cortisol suppression (≤0.9 µg/dL), suggesting they are not metabolically benign. These findings challenge the implicit assumption that any post-DST cortisol ≤1.8 µg/dL represents a uniform 'no-risk' category.
items.caveat: Cross-sectional design precludes causal inference or outcome data; sample sizes per group are small (n=48–60), and the study is retrospective with potential for unmeasured confounders. Prospective longitudinal validation with hard cardiovascular endpoints is needed before any threshold revision is justified.
items.quiz_question: A 55-year-old man with hypertension and dyslipidemia has a 1.8 cm right adrenal incidentaloma. His post-1 mg DST cortisol returns at 1.4 µg/dL—below the conventional MACS cutoff. His internist asks if he needs any additional evaluation given 'normal' cortisol suppression. How do you respond based on current data?
items.quiz_answer: According to this study, patients with post-DST cortisol in the 0.91–1.79 µg/dL range display an intermediate cardiometabolic phenotype—with meaningfully higher blood pressure, HbA1c, and LDL than patients with cortisol ≤0.9 µg/dL—despite falling below the MACS diagnostic threshold. This patient should not be reassured that his cardiometabolic risk is equivalent to complete suppressors; aggressive risk factor management is warranted, and the findings support ongoing clinical vigilance rather than dismissal.

items.title: Predictors of overall mortality in pituitary adenomas.
items.summary: This retrospective analysis of 699 patients across four major pituitary adenoma subtypes (acromegaly, Cushing's disease, macroprolactinoma, non-functioning macroadenoma) found that age at diagnosis was the single most consistent predictor of overall mortality, with a hazard ratio of 1.07–1.11 per year across all subtypes. Cushing's disease carried independent mortality risk. Notably, hypopituitarism predicted increased mortality only in non-functioning macroadenomas (HR 2.71), but was paradoxically associated with reduced mortality in acromegaly—possibly reflecting ascertainment bias or more intensive follow-up in hypopituitary acromegaly patients. Sex, tumor size, and radiotherapy were not independently associated with mortality.
items.caveat: Retrospective single-center design with relatively small numbers in the Cushing's disease subgroup (n=42), limiting power for subgroup analyses. Causality of hypopituitarism's divergent effects across subtypes is speculative; confounding by indication (e.g., more aggressive tumors receiving radiotherapy) cannot be excluded.
items.quiz_question: You are counseling a 68-year-old man newly diagnosed with a non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma. He asks about his long-term prognosis. Endocrine workup reveals partial hypopituitarism affecting the GH and gonadal axes. Based on this study, does his hypopituitarism status alter his mortality risk, and what is the dominant overall mortality predictor across all pituitary adenoma subtypes?
items.quiz_answer: According to this study, hypopituitarism in the setting of non-functioning macroadenomas was associated with a significantly increased mortality risk (HR 2.71), making it an important prognostic factor in this specific subtype—unlike in acromegaly, where the association was inverse. Across all subtypes, however, age at diagnosis was the dominant and most consistent predictor of mortality (HR 1.07–1.11 per year), underscoring the importance of close long-term follow-up and complete hormone replacement in older patients with NFMA and hypopituitarism.
items.journal: Experimental and clinical endocrinology & diabetes : official journal, German Society of Endocrinology [and] German Diabetes Association

items.title: Prevalence and clinical relevance of negative histology after transsphenoidal surgery for pituitary neuroendocrine tumors.
items.summary: In a retrospective series of 651 patients undergoing transsphenoidal surgery, negative histology (NH) — normal pituitary tissue on pathology despite clinical/biochemical/radiological evidence of tumor — occurred in 28.1% of ACTH- and PRL-secreting microadenomas and 11.4% of GH tumors. Early remission rates were significantly lower in NH versus positive-histology cases for both ACTH (60% vs. 93.2%) and PRL (50% vs. 79.3%) tumors, but not for GH tumors. Mislocalization of the tumor at surgery accounted for two-thirds of unfavorable ACTH-NH outcomes, underscoring that NH is not a uniform entity but arises from distinct mechanisms — mislocalization, technical sampling error, or histological limitations — that vary by tumor subtype. For GH-secreting tumors, NH appears to carry a favorable prognosis, likely reflecting sampling limitations rather than true surgical failure.
items.caveat: Single-center retrospective design spanning nearly three decades, with possible evolution in surgical technique and immunohistochemistry protocols over time. ACTH microadenoma cohort sizes for the NH subgroup were not specified numerically beyond percentages, limiting precision of remission rate comparisons.
items.quiz_question: A 32-year-old woman undergoes transsphenoidal surgery for biochemically confirmed Cushing's disease (elevated UFC, abnormal DST, IPSS lateralization to the right). Intraoperative exploration reveals no discrete adenoma; pathology returns normal corticotroph tissue. What does the literature suggest about her likelihood of early remission compared with a patient whose pathology shows an ACTH-positive adenoma, and what mechanism most likely explains her negative histology?
items.quiz_answer: Based on this study, early remission rates in ACTH-negative histology cases are approximately 60%, compared with ~93% when an adenoma is confirmed on pathology. The predominant mechanism — accounting for roughly two-thirds of unfavorable NH outcomes in ACTH tumors — is surgical mislocalization: the tumor exists but was not correctly identified or resected during exploration. This is distinct from GH-NH, where negative histology more often reflects technical or sampling limitations and carries a favorable prognosis.

items.title: A two-centre experience with hand-assisted laparoscopic, transperitoneal laparoscopic and retroperitoneoscopic adrenalectomy.
items.summary: In one of the largest comparative series to date (444 patients across two tertiary centers, 2009–2025), hand-assisted laparoscopic (HAL) adrenalectomy was used selectively for larger, more complex tumors (median 6.5 cm) and malignancies, achieving shorter operative times than transperitoneal laparoscopic (TL) despite greater lesion complexity, but at the cost of higher postoperative complication rates (16.5% vs. 7.6% TL vs. 8.8% RP). Retroperitoneoscopic (RP) adrenalectomy demonstrated the lowest complication rate and shortest hospital stay for smaller benign lesions, consistent with current guideline preference. Pheochromocytomas were managed predominantly by HAL and TL, with conversion rates of ~5–6% across approaches due to hemorrhage and difficult dissection.
items.caveat: Retrospective two-center design with inherent selection bias — HAL cases were systematically selected for larger and more malignant lesions, making complication rate comparisons across techniques confounded by case complexity. Robotic adrenalectomy was not included, limiting contemporary relevance.
items.quiz_question: You are planning adrenalectomy for a 58-year-old with a 7 cm right adrenal mass that is biochemically consistent with pheochromocytoma and appears confined on imaging. Which surgical approach does this two-center series suggest was most commonly employed for pheochromocytomas, and what is the approximate conversion-to-open rate you should counsel the patient about?
items.quiz_answer: According to this series, pheochromocytomas were most commonly managed using hand-assisted laparoscopic (HAL, 31.8%) and transperitoneal laparoscopic (TL, 27.5%) approaches. The conversion rate to open surgery was approximately 5.9% for HAL (primarily due to hemorrhage and local invasion) and 5.8% for TL (hemorrhage, difficult dissection, unclear anatomy) — both figures the patient should be counseled about preoperatively.

items.title: Prevalence of Adrenal Insufficiency in Clinically Stable Adults Living with HIV Attending Outpatient Clinics in Malaysia.
items.summary: In a cross-sectional study of 110 clinically stable HIV-positive outpatients on HAART, adrenal insufficiency (AI) identified by cosyntropin stimulation test was found in only 1.8% (95% CI 0.2–6.4%), lower than many prior estimates. Both patients with AI had negative adrenal antibodies and ACTH levels suggesting primary adrenal origin; they were significantly more likely to have lower nadir CD4 counts, a history of treatment failure, and symptoms suggestive of AI. These findings suggest routine AI screening in all stable HIV patients on effective HAART may not be warranted, but targeted evaluation in those with relevant risk factors remains prudent.
items.caveat: Small sample size (n=110) yields very wide confidence intervals around the 1.8% prevalence estimate, limiting generalizability. Cross-sectional design, single-country population, and the use of a single cosyntropin stimulation test without cortisol day-curve or insulin tolerance testing may miss subtle secondary AI. Possible selection bias toward healthier patients attending stable outpatient clinics.
items.quiz_question: A 44-year-old man with well-controlled HIV (viral load undetectable, current CD4 800 cells/mm³) is referred for fatigue and mild hyperpigmentation. His nadir CD4 was 45 cells/mm³ and he had two prior treatment failures before achieving viral suppression. Based on this Malaysian study, which clinical features would most support proceeding with cosyntropin stimulation testing in this patient?
items.quiz_answer: The study identified three significant predictors of AI in stable HIV patients: lower nadir CD4 count, a history of antiretroviral treatment failure, and symptoms suggestive of adrenal insufficiency (e.g., fatigue, hyperpigmentation, weight loss). This patient has all three risk factors — a very low nadir CD4 (45 cells/mm³), two prior treatment failures, and clinical symptoms — making him an appropriate candidate for cosyntropin stimulation testing despite his current viral suppression.
items.journal: Journal of the ASEAN Federation of Endocrine Societies

items.title: Predictors of in vitro response to somatostatin and dopamine receptor-targeted treatments are lacking in clinically non-functioning pituitary tumors.
items.summary: In a series of 44 NF-PitNET primary cultures, overall cell-proliferation inhibition with somatostatin receptor ligands (octreotide, pasireotide) and dopamine agonists was negligible (median reduction 4–7%), though roughly 30% of individual cultures qualified as responders to at least one agent. SSTR2 expression correlated with octreotide and pasireotide efficacy, and both D2R and SSTR2 expression discriminated responders to the chimeric SSTR2/SSTR5/D2R ligand BIM-23B065 with acceptable AUC (~0.74–0.78). However, no standard clinical or pathological parameter—including tumor grade, Ki67, invasiveness, or receptor expression in aggregate—reliably predicted which tumors would respond, underscoring the absence of a clinically actionable biomarker for medical therapy in this setting.
items.caveat: In vitro proliferation assays may not faithfully reflect in vivo drug behavior; sample size is modest (n=44) and the work is single-center, limiting generalizability. The 20% inhibition threshold defining 'responder' is somewhat arbitrary.
items.quiz_question: A 62-year-old man has a residual non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma after transsphenoidal surgery. Immunohistochemistry shows high D2R (IRS 8) and moderate SSTR2 (IRS 4) expression. Based on this study's findings, which medical agent shows the most promise as a rational candidate, and what is the key limitation of relying on receptor expression to guide that choice?
items.quiz_answer: The chimeric ligand BIM-23B065 (targeting SSTR2, SSTR5, and D2R) showed the most discriminating response based on D2R and SSTR2 expression (AUC ~0.74–0.78). However, the study found that no standard tumor parameter—including receptor expression—robustly predicted response across the whole cohort, meaning receptor staining alone is insufficient to guarantee clinical benefit; overall in vitro inhibition even for 'responders' averaged only ~20–28%.

items.title: Endoscopic Endonasal Versus Endoscopic Supraorbital Keyhole Surgery for Craniopharyngioma Resection: A 15-Year Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study.
items.summary: In this 15-year retrospective cohort of 60 patients with craniopharyngioma, the endoscopic endonasal approach (EEA) achieved gross-total resection in 83% versus 60% for the supraorbital keyhole approach (SOK), with visual improvement in 87% versus 63%—both statistically significant differences. CSF leak was more frequent with EEA (13% vs. 3%), while endocrine deficit rates and recurrence did not differ significantly between groups. The authors emphasize that case allocation was not random: midline suprasellar/intrasellar tumors were preferentially assigned to EEA, which substantially confounds the comparison.
items.caveat: This is a non-randomized, single-center retrospective study with significant selection bias—tumor anatomy drove approach selection, making direct outcome comparisons between groups inherently confounded. Endocrine deficit data were reported only descriptively without statistical comparison, which is a meaningful gap for endocrinologists tracking postoperative pituitary function.
items.quiz_question: A 45-year-old woman with a suprasellar craniopharyngioma (intrasellar extension, no retrochiasmatic involvement) is being counseled on surgical approach. Based on this study, what are the relative advantages of the endoscopic endonasal approach over the supraorbital keyhole route, and what is the main complication trade-off to communicate?
items.quiz_answer: The EEA was associated with higher gross-total resection rates (83% vs. 60%) and better visual improvement (87% vs. 63%) for midline tumors. The main trade-off is a higher CSF leak rate with EEA (13% vs. 3%), which requires reconstruction strategies and carries risk of meningitis. Endocrine deficits did not significantly differ, though these data were not statistically analyzed in detail.
items.journal: JPMA. The Journal of the Pakistan Medical Association

items.title: Management of Adrenal Incidentalomas: A Survey of Physicians from the Middle East and Africa.
items.summary: This survey of 171 physicians (71% endocrinologists) from the Middle East and Africa reveals two persistent practice gaps: underappreciation of malignancy risk for adrenal masses >4 cm (only 64% flagged size >4 cm as a malignancy signal, and only 20% recognized that a confirmed benign-appearing mass on unenhanced CT requires no further imaging), and over-investigation of biochemically and radiologically confirmed benign tumors (56% recommended repeated biochemical testing and 43% favored 4–5 years of follow-up regardless of imaging features). Screening for the three major functional syndromes (hypercortisolism, pheochromocytoma, primary aldosteronism) was near-universal, which aligns with guideline recommendations.
items.caveat: Survey-based study with inherent response and selection bias; 171 respondents from a large and heterogeneous geographic region may not represent actual practice patterns. Guideline adherence questions used simplified vignette framing that may not capture real-world clinical complexity.
items.quiz_question: You are reviewing adrenal incidentaloma management at a quality-improvement meeting. Based on this regional survey, which two guideline-discordant behaviors are most prevalent among endocrinologists in this region, and what is the correct guideline-concordant approach for each?
items.quiz_answer: The two main gaps are: (1) underestimating malignancy risk for masses >4 cm—guidelines recommend surgical referral for adrenal masses >4 cm even without overt hormonal activity due to elevated malignancy risk; and (2) over-investigating confirmed benign, nonfunctioning incidentalomas with repeated biochemical and imaging follow-up—current guidelines (e.g., ESE/ENSAT 2023) support limiting or discontinuing surveillance after establishing a benign radiological phenotype (e.g., homogeneous, <10 HU on unenhanced CT, <4 cm) with a single normal biochemical evaluation.

items.title: Association of Post-Dexamethasone Cortisol With Cardiovascular and Metabolic Comorbidities in Patients With Nonfunctioning Adrenal Adenomas.
items.summary: In a retrospective single-center study of 444 adults with radiographically confirmed nonfunctioning adrenal adenomas (post-1mg DST cortisol ≤1.8 µg/dL), each 0.1 µg/dL increment in post-DST cortisol within the 'suppressed' range was independently associated with 21% higher odds of documented ASCVD and 24% higher odds of metabolic syndrome. The exploratory Youden-optimal threshold was ~0.985 µg/dL, with 87% sensitivity and 92% NPV for ASCVD, and the ROC AUC was 0.820. These findings suggest a continuous cardiometabolic gradient exists even below conventional MACS thresholds, challenging the binary 'suppressed vs. not suppressed' framing clinicians currently apply to NFAAs.
items.caveat: Retrospective single-center design with potential referral bias; the Youden-optimal cutoff is exploratory and the authors explicitly caution against its use as a diagnostic threshold without prospective validation. Causality cannot be established from this design.
items.quiz_question: A 60-year-old woman with a 2.8 cm left adrenal adenoma (HU ≤10, no hormonal excess on standard workup) has a post-1mg DST cortisol of 1.1 µg/dL — well within the 'suppressed' range. Based on this study, how should you counsel her regarding cardiometabolic risk?
items.quiz_answer: Even within the conventionally suppressed range, higher post-DST cortisol values carry independently higher odds of ASCVD and metabolic syndrome. A cortisol of 1.1 µg/dL sits above the exploratory threshold of ~0.985 µg/dL identified in this study. Clinicians should ensure aggressive cardiometabolic risk factor screening and management in such patients, recognizing a potential subclinical cortisol-driven gradient rather than assuming reassurance from a 'normal' suppression result.
items.journal: Endocrine practice : official journal of the American College of Endocrinology and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists

items.title: 'Paraganglioma and pheochromocytoma: a review of current guidelines, new diagnostic and therapeutic approaches'.
items.summary: This review synthesizes more than ten new consensus statements on pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma (PPGL) published since 2022, reflecting a rapidly evolving field. Key paradigm shifts highlighted include the adoption of a genotype-first clinical approach (given up to 40% hereditary cases), dedicated pediatric protocols, updated histopathological classification criteria, advanced targeted therapeutics, and novel predictive tools. The unified reclassification of pheochromocytomas as intra-adrenal paragangliomas is also discussed as framing all PPGLs within a single disease spectrum.
items.caveat: This is a narrative review article without systematic methodology, so evidence weighting across the cited consensus statements is not explicitly graded. Readers should consult primary guidelines for strength-of-evidence ratings on specific recommendations.
items.quiz_question: A 28-year-old woman is found to have a right adrenal pheochromocytoma on workup for hypertension. Her plasma metanephrines are elevated. She has no family history of endocrine tumors. Per current genotype-first guidelines, what is the recommended next step beyond standard biochemical confirmation and imaging localization?
items.quiz_answer: Germline genetic testing should be offered to all patients with confirmed PPGL regardless of family history, as up to 40% of cases are driven by hereditary germline mutations. Identifying the specific susceptibility gene (e.g., SDHB, SDHD, VHL, RET, NF1) directly dictates surgical strategy, surveillance intervals, screening of at-risk relatives, and risk of malignancy.

items.title: Functional analysis of adrenocorticotropic-hormone-producing pituitary cells derived from human pluripotent stem cells in murine and primate models of hypopituitarism.
items.summary: This study transplanted human embryonic stem cell-derived pituitary-hypothalamus organoids subcutaneously into hypopituitary SCID mice and a hypopituitary cynomolgus monkey, demonstrating that the organoids survived >6 months in mice, significantly improved circulating ACTH levels, and prolonged survival compared to sham controls. In the non-human primate model, organoids remained functional for 6 weeks and raised ACTH concentrations under immunosuppression modeled on clinical islet transplantation protocols. The authors describe this as the first demonstration of efficacious pituitary cell transplantation in a primate, offering a potential path toward physiologically responsive ACTH replacement that could mitigate crisis risk in hypopituitarism.
items.caveat: This is a small-scale proof-of-concept study — only a single non-human primate was used for the primate model, and durability beyond 6 weeks in primates is unknown. Human clinical translation requires extensive additional safety, immunosuppression optimization, and manufacturing scale-up data. Results should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating only.
items.quiz_question: A 35-year-old man with panhypopituitarism from a prior craniopharyngioma resection struggles with recurrent adrenal crises despite education and sick-day dosing. He asks about emerging therapies beyond hydrocortisone replacement. How would you contextualize the potential of pituitary cell transplantation based on current evidence?
items.quiz_answer: Pituitary-hypothalamus organoids derived from pluripotent stem cells have shown proof-of-concept in rodent and, very preliminarily, primate models, restoring ACTH production and improving survival. However, this remains far from clinical application — no human trials exist, primate data come from a single animal with only 6 weeks of follow-up, and challenges including immunosuppression, manufacturing scale-up, and long-term safety remain unresolved. This should be framed to the patient as an exciting but distant future direction, not an imminent option.

items.title: Pituitary metastases: a real-world single-center surgical cohort.
items.summary: This retrospective single-center series of 19 histologically confirmed pituitary metastases (2000–2025) found that neuro-ophthalmological symptoms were the dominant presentation (84%), while AVP deficiency (diabetes insipidus) occurred in 37% and isolated ACTH deficiency in 33% of those with hormonal compromise. Lung and breast primaries predominated, and in 21% of cases the pituitary was the index site identifying the underlying malignancy. Median overall survival after surgery was only 23.5 months, and 87.5% of patients with available data had residual or recurrent disease post-resection, underscoring the palliative intent of surgery in most cases.
items.caveat: Single-center retrospective cohort of only 19 patients spanning 25 years; selection bias toward surgically managed cases means the true epidemiology of pituitary metastases is likely underrepresented. No control group or outcome comparison with non-surgical management.
items.quiz_question: A 62-year-old woman with a known history of breast cancer presents with sudden-onset diabetes insipidus and bitemporal hemianopia. MRI shows a sellar mass with involvement of the pituitary stalk. Based on this series, what is the most likely diagnosis, and what additional hormonal deficiency pattern should you actively screen for?
items.quiz_answer: Pituitary metastasis should be the leading diagnosis given the known primary malignancy, stalk involvement, and DI (AVP deficiency occurred in 37% of cases in this series). You should screen for isolated ACTH deficiency, which was the single most common anterior pituitary hormone deficiency identified (6/12 patients with any deficiency), as well as full anterior pituitary axis evaluation given that pan-hypopituitarism occurred in ~17%.

items.title: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-related endocrinopathies: from immune crosstalk to predictive biomarkers and precision management.
items.summary: This narrative review synthesizes current mechanistic understanding of ICI-induced endocrine toxicities, with particular focus on hypophysitis and adrenal insufficiency as the pituitary/adrenal manifestations. It highlights that adrenal insufficiency from ICI therapy is often irreversible and may lack early warning signs, making it particularly dangerous in ambulatory cancer patients. The review discusses emerging predictive biomarkers—including thyroid autoantibodies, cytokine profiles, and single-cell sequencing—as well as liquid biopsy and imaging-based tools, framing these within a 'proactive endocrine protection' paradigm that emphasizes moving from reactive toxicity management to earlier individualized surveillance.
items.caveat: Narrative review design with inherent selection bias; most cited biomarkers are exploratory and lack prospective validation. The authors explicitly acknowledge the need for large-scale prospective studies before clinical implementation of any predictive model.
items.quiz_question: A 58-year-old man receiving combination ipilimumab/nivolumab for metastatic melanoma develops fatigue, hyponatremia, and a morning cortisol of 4 µg/dL at week 8. He has no headache or visual symptoms. Based on current evidence reviewed in this paper, what is the key distinction you must make before initiating corticosteroid replacement, and why does it matter prognostically?
items.quiz_answer: You must distinguish primary adrenal insufficiency (ICI-induced adrenalitis, typically irreversible) from secondary adrenal insufficiency due to ICI-induced hypophysitis (which may partially recover with corticosteroid treatment of the hypophysitis itself). This distinction matters because hypophysitis-related secondary AI may show partial pituitary recovery, whereas primary adrenal insufficiency from ICI therapy is typically permanent and requires lifelong glucocorticoid (and often mineralocorticoid) replacement. ACTH level and full anterior pituitary axis testing, along with adrenal imaging, are needed to differentiate these.

items.title: Analysis of the clinical profile of multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes and the association with other tumors.
items.summary: In this registry-based chart review of 182 MEN patients (106 MEN1, 76 MEN2), the classical tumor associations were confirmed—parathyroid (90%), pituitary (61%), and GEP-NETs (65%) in MEN1; MTC (61%), pheochromocytoma (32%), and hyperparathyroidism (15%) in MEN2. Notably, a substantial proportion of patients in both groups harbored tumors not classically associated with their syndrome, including papillary thyroid cancer in MEN1 (5.7%), renal cell carcinoma in MEN1 (4.7%), and breast cancer and lymphoma in both syndromes, raising questions about whether MEN1 and RET mutations may contribute more broadly to tumorigenesis than currently recognized.
items.caveat: Retrospective chart review from a single institution with only clinical (not uniformly genetic) criteria for syndrome classification; association does not establish causation, and concurrent sporadic malignancies cannot be excluded. Genetically confirmed cases were a subset (45 MEN1, 69 MEN2), limiting mechanistic conclusions.
items.quiz_question: A 45-year-old woman with genetically confirmed MEN1 (MEN1 mutation) presents for routine surveillance. She has known parathyroid disease and a small non-functioning pituitary adenoma. She mentions a recent breast lump. Based on this registry analysis, how should you counsel her regarding breast cancer risk in MEN1?
items.quiz_answer: This series found breast cancer in 1.9% of MEN1 patients, a rate that may exceed what would be expected by chance, though causality is unproven. The authors conclude that further investigation is needed to clarify whether MEN1 mutations contribute to breast tumorigenesis. While current guidelines do not mandate enhanced breast cancer screening specifically for MEN1, this finding supports a low threshold for prompt evaluation of any breast mass and warrants discussion in the context of her overall surveillance plan.
items.journal: Endocrine practice : official journal of the American College of Endocrinology and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists

items.title: GATA3-positive silent corticotroph adenomas are characterized by large size and massive infrasellar invasion.
items.summary: In a cohort of 45 silent corticotroph adenomas (SCAs), roughly one quarter (11/45) were GATA3-positive, and this subgroup was significantly more likely to be male, to present as giant adenomas (82% vs. 24%), and to demonstrate massive sphenoid/infrasellar invasion. Despite their more locally aggressive radiological phenotype, GATA3-positive SCAs did not show higher Ki-67, more mitoses, or worse post-surgical outcomes compared to GATA3-negative tumors. Importantly, gross total resection was achieved in none of the GATA3-positive cases versus about one-third of the GATA3-negative cases, underscoring a surgically challenging profile. These findings suggest GATA3 immunostaining may help risk-stratify SCAs preoperatively and set expectations for surgical completeness.
items.caveat: Single-center retrospective study with only 11 GATA3-positive cases; the lack of a statistically significant difference in post-surgical outcomes may reflect insufficient power rather than true equivalence. Long-term recurrence data are limited.
items.quiz_question: A 52-year-old man undergoes transsphenoidal resection of a large sellar mass found to be a silent corticotroph adenoma on pathology. Immunostaining returns GATA3-positive. Which preoperative radiological feature and surgical outcome would you most expect based on this molecular subtype?
items.quiz_answer: GATA3-positive silent corticotroph adenomas are disproportionately associated with giant tumor size and massive infrasellar (sphenoid sinus) invasion. Gross total resection is significantly less likely in this subgroup (0% in this series vs. ~32% in GATA3-negative tumors), so the patient and surgical team should be counseled about a higher likelihood of residual disease and the potential need for adjuvant therapy.

items.title: Approach to the pregnant patient with prolactinoma.
items.summary: This clinical review provides a practical framework for managing prolactinoma across the preconception, pregnancy, and postpartum continuum. Key points include that cabergoline is increasingly preferred over bromocriptine for its superior efficacy and tolerability, and that either agent can be safely restarted if symptomatic tumor enlargement occurs during pregnancy. Pituitary apoplexy, though rare, may require glucocorticoid replacement or transsphenoidal surgery depending on neuro-ophthalmological severity. Breastfeeding is generally permitted, and dopamine agonists should be withheld during lactation unless clinically necessary.
items.caveat: This is a narrative review without a formal systematic methodology; recommendations reflect expert consensus and existing observational data rather than randomized trial evidence. Individual risk-benefit assessment remains essential, particularly for macroadenomas.
items.quiz_question: A 29-year-old woman with a known macroprolactinoma on cabergoline achieves pregnancy after stopping the drug. At 22 weeks, she develops worsening headaches and bitemporal visual field constriction on confrontation testing. What is your next management step?
items.quiz_answer: Symptomatic tumor enlargement during pregnancy warrants prompt formal visual field testing and MRI (without gadolinium). If clinically significant growth is confirmed, dopamine agonist therapy—preferably cabergoline given its efficacy and tolerability profile—should be restarted. Transsphenoidal surgery is reserved for cases refractory to medical therapy or with severe, rapidly progressive neuro-ophthalmological compromise.
items.journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

items.title: Malignancy in patients with acromegaly: a multicenter study across the Gulf region.
items.summary: This multicenter retrospective study of 157 acromegaly patients across five Gulf tertiary centers found a 6.4% overall malignancy rate, with papillary thyroid carcinoma comprising 8 of 10 cases. Patients with malignancy were significantly older (mean 56.6 vs. 46.5 years), and all ultimately achieved remission or excellent response at last follow-up. The authors conclude that findings support individualized, symptom- and risk-factor-driven cancer surveillance rather than an acromegaly-specific screening program.
items.caveat: Critically limited by only 10 malignancy events, retrospective design, no population comparator, and nonstandardized cancer testing across centers—making detection and selection bias highly plausible. The predominance of papillary thyroid carcinoma may partly reflect incidental detection bias given co-incident thyroid imaging. No firm conclusions about excess malignancy risk can be drawn.
items.quiz_question: A 58-year-old man with well-controlled acromegaly asks whether he needs routine cancer screening beyond standard population guidelines. Based on available multicenter regional data, what is the most evidence-supported approach to malignancy surveillance in acromegaly?
items.quiz_answer: Current evidence—including this Gulf multicenter cohort—does not support a disease-specific blanket cancer screening protocol for acromegaly. Surveillance should be individualized based on age, family history, symptoms, and adherence to population-level guidelines (e.g., colonoscopy per standard colorectal screening recommendations). The predominant associated malignancy observed was papillary thyroid carcinoma, often incidentally detected, but routine thyroid screening beyond what is clinically indicated is not yet evidence-supported.

items.title: Patient-reported measures in hypothalamic-pituitary diseases.
items.summary: This comprehensive review synthesizes available PREMs (Patient-Reported Experience Measures) and PROMs (Patient-Reported Outcome Measures) across the major hypothalamic-pituitary conditions, including Cushing's disease, acromegaly, prolactinoma, non-functioning pituitary adenoma, hypopituitarism (including GH and AVP deficiencies), and craniopharyngioma. A consistent finding is that biochemical and hormonal control after medical or surgical treatment improves health-related quality of life (HRQoL), but HRQoL often remains below that of healthy controls even after successful treatment. Notably, the review highlights a systematic mismatch between what patients report as most burdensome and what clinicians prioritize, underscoring the value of formally integrating patient-reported tools into routine pituitary disease follow-up.
items.caveat: This is a narrative review without a formal systematic review methodology or meta-analysis; heterogeneity across included studies and instruments limits definitive conclusions about which PROM best captures disease burden for any given pituitary condition.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old woman with biochemically remitted Cushing's disease (post-transsphenoidal surgery, UFC normal for 2 years) continues to report significant fatigue, cognitive difficulties, and reduced quality of life. Based on the literature reviewed in this paper, how should her care team interpret and address this?
items.quiz_answer: This presentation is consistent with the review's finding that HRQoL often remains impaired below healthy-control levels even after successful hormonal remission in Cushing's disease. Clinicians should not equate biochemical remission with patient recovery; formal PROM assessment should be incorporated to identify and address residual domains of impairment (e.g., fatigue, mood, cognitive function), which patients and providers frequently weight differently.

items.title: Pheochromocytoma Across the Perioperative Course: Current Concepts and Clinical Management.
items.summary: This narrative review provides an updated, anesthesia-focused framework for perioperative pheochromocytoma management, integrating contemporary evidence on catecholamine-induced cardiovascular dysfunction, intraoperative hemodynamic crises, fluid and vasoactive therapy, and post-resection complications including hypoglycemia and vasoplegia. A dedicated section addresses the high-risk scenario of previously undiagnosed pheochromocytoma presenting during unrelated surgery, recommending that nonessential procedures be aborted once intraoperative suspicion arises and immediate stabilization prioritized. The review also covers medication-triggered crises and the importance of multidisciplinary perioperative coordination involving the endocrinologist, anesthesiologist, surgeon, and cardiologist.
items.caveat: As a narrative review, this paper does not provide new primary data or a systematic literature search; recommendations are synthesized from existing evidence of varying quality and should be contextualized against individual institutional protocols and patient-specific factors.
items.quiz_question: A 52-year-old man with an undiagnosed right adrenal pheochromocytoma undergoes elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Shortly after insufflation, he develops severe hypertension (220/130 mmHg) with tachycardia. According to the perioperative management framework described in this review, what should be the immediate priority?
items.quiz_answer: Immediate hemodynamic stabilization is the priority. The review recommends that once intraoperative pheochromocytoma is suspected, the surgical team should be notified promptly, and the decision to abort versus continue should be based on the urgency of the operation and the patient's clinical status—in most cases, nonessential surgery should be aborted. Intraoperative hypertension should be managed with short-acting antihypertensives (e.g., phentolamine, nicardipine, or sodium nitroprusside), and the patient should be transitioned to a monitored setting for further evaluation and planned definitive resection after appropriate alpha-blockade.

items.title: Arginine vasopressin deficiency revealing a disseminated human chorionic gonadotropin-secreting germinoma.
items.summary: This case report describes a 20-year-old male presenting with AVP deficiency (central diabetes insipidus) in whom initial pituitary MRI showed a small enhancing lesion with pituitary stalk thickening, but extensive workup for inflammatory and infiltrative etiologies was unrevealing. Transsphenoidal biopsy ultimately confirmed an hCG-secreting germinoma, and subsequent staging revealed disseminated disease requiring craniospinal irradiation. The case reinforces that pituitary stalk thickening with AVP-D in a young patient mandates a low threshold for biopsy and tumor marker assessment (serum/CSF beta-hCG and AFP) even when initial workup is negative, as germinoma can present with deceptively subtle or inconclusive imaging.
items.caveat: Single case report; no generalizability data. However, it illustrates a well-recognized but frequently delayed diagnostic pitfall in the evaluation of central AVP deficiency with stalk thickening, consistent with existing guideline-level guidance on this workup.
items.quiz_question: A 19-year-old male presents with 6 months of polyuria and polydipsia. Water deprivation test and desmopressin response confirm AVP deficiency. MRI shows pituitary stalk thickening and a small enhancing sellar lesion. Autoimmune panel and ACE level are negative. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step according to the approach illustrated in this case?
items.quiz_answer: Serum and CSF beta-hCG and AFP should be measured to evaluate for a secreting germinoma, and if inconclusive, pituitary/stalk biopsy should be strongly considered. As illustrated in this case, germinomas can present with subtle imaging findings and negative initial inflammatory workup; biopsy provided the definitive diagnosis of an hCG-secreting germinoma with disseminated disease, enabling appropriate craniospinal irradiation.

items.title: Iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome from an adulterated glucocorticoid-containing supplement.
items.summary: A man in his 40s developed clinical and biochemical Cushing's syndrome with suppressed cortisol and ACTH after using a joint-pain supplement (Artri King Reforzado Con Ortiga Y Omega 3) that had been FDA-recalled for undeclared dexamethasone. Symptoms emerged after supplement discontinuation — consistent with secondary adrenal insufficiency from exogenous glucocorticoid — and resolved with hydrocortisone replacement. This case underscores that adulterated over-the-counter supplements are a clinically meaningful cause of iatrogenic Cushing's and secondary adrenal insufficiency that requires proactive history-taking.
items.caveat: Single case report; causation is strongly implied by temporal association and FDA recall data but individual dexamethasone dose/duration was not quantified. Publication bias toward dramatic presentations means milder supplement-induced HPA suppression is likely underreported.
items.quiz_question: A 45-year-old man presents with 3 months of progressive centripetal weight gain, abdominal striae, and fatigue. Morning serum cortisol is 1.2 mcg/dL and ACTH is undetectable. He denies prescription steroid use. What is the most critical next step in the history, and what diagnosis should you consider?
items.quiz_answer: Ask specifically about all supplements, herbal remedies, and over-the-counter products for pain or inflammation. Adulterated supplements containing undeclared glucocorticoids (such as dexamethasone, as documented in the FDA-recalled Artri King product) can cause iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome with secondary adrenal insufficiency. Hydrocortisone replacement should be initiated after discontinuing the offending agent while awaiting HPA axis recovery.

items.title: Clinical Implications and Research Progress of Salivary Biomarkers for Endocrine and Metabolic Disorders.
items.summary: This comprehensive review synthesizes evidence on salivary biomarkers for endocrine and metabolic assessment, identifying late-night salivary cortisol (LNSC) as the most clinically established marker — guideline-endorsed for Cushing's syndrome — with salivary cortisone potentially offering incremental diagnostic accuracy. Most other salivary biomarkers (glycemic markers, adipokines, uric acid) remain exploratory, limited by inconsistent collection protocols, oral disease confounders, and lack of standardized analytical platforms. The authors advocate for large-scale multicentre validation and standardized procedures before broader clinical adoption.
items.caveat: Narrative review methodology with inherent selection bias; many included studies are small or observational. Clinical cutoffs for salivary cortisone in Cushing's diagnosis are not yet guideline-validated, and confounders such as oral inflammation, smoking, and medication effects on salivary gland function are incompletely controlled across the reviewed literature.
items.quiz_question: You are evaluating a 38-year-old woman for possible Cushing's syndrome. She asks whether saliva testing is a reliable alternative to 24-hour UFC or late-night serum cortisol. Based on current evidence, how would you counsel her, and what is the most validated salivary test for this indication?
items.quiz_answer: Late-night salivary cortisol (LNSC) is the most clinically established and guideline-endorsed salivary biomarker for Cushing's syndrome, reflecting the loss of normal nocturnal cortisol nadir. Salivary cortisone may add diagnostic accuracy but is not yet guideline-validated. Key caveats include the need for proper collection technique, avoidance of oral bleeding or food, and awareness that oral disease or certain medications can confound results. LNSC is a reasonable first-line screening test but not the sole modality.

items.title: Predicting early recurrence of craniopharyngioma using multi-omics radiomic modeling: a retrospective cohort study.
items.summary: This single-center retrospective study of 106 surgically treated craniopharyngioma patients developed a habitat-based multimodal MRI radiomics model to predict early postoperative recurrence. The best-performing Combined model achieved AUCs of 0.944 (training) and 0.891 (validation), with SHAP analysis identifying T1C-derived and H3-related habitat features — thought to reflect intratumoral heterogeneity — as the strongest predictors. If externally validated, such a model could help risk-stratify patients for adjuvant therapy or intensified surveillance after surgery.
items.caveat: Retrospective single-center design with a modest sample of 106 patients significantly limits generalizability; the authors themselves label findings as preliminary pending multicenter validation. Radiomics models are highly sensitive to MRI acquisition parameters and scanner variability, which were not addressed in this cohort.
items.quiz_question: A 32-year-old patient undergoes gross total resection of a craniopharyngioma. You are counseling about recurrence risk and surveillance strategy. What imaging features from this radiomics study were most strongly associated with early recurrence, and how might this type of modeling eventually influence post-operative management?
items.quiz_answer: T1C-derived (contrast-enhanced T1) and H3-related habitat features — radiomics signatures capturing intratumoral spatial heterogeneity in the peripheral tumor subregion — were the strongest predictors of early recurrence in this model. If validated in multicenter cohorts, such models could identify high-risk patients who might benefit from more aggressive adjuvant therapy (e.g., radiotherapy) or shorter surveillance imaging intervals, rather than applying a uniform post-operative strategy to all craniopharyngioma patients.

items.title: Prolactinomas in women of reproductive age: a proposed reproductive-intent-based framework for diagnosis and management.
items.summary: This narrative mini-review proposes a reproductive-intent-based framework for managing prolactinomas in women of reproductive age, organizing care into three dynamic states: fertility-driven, endocrine-stabilization, and surveillance-dominant. It emphasizes that tumor-related risk factors—optic apparatus proximity, documented growth, apoplexy, and dopamine agonist resistance—serve as cross-cutting safety modifiers that can shift a patient between states. The authors reinforce that persistent hyperprolactinemia alone, without clinically meaningful hypogonadism, symptoms, or tumor progression, does not necessarily justify therapy. Dopamine agonists remain first-line; surgery is reserved for anatomically favorable tumors or medical treatment failure.
items.caveat: This is a narrative review proposing a clinical framework, not a validated prediction rule or guideline; the authors explicitly note it requires prospective validation and does not replace existing guideline-based recommendations.
items.quiz_question: A 29-year-old woman with a 6 mm microprolactinoma is incidentally found to have a serum prolactin of 68 ng/mL. She has regular menses, no galactorrhea, and is not currently seeking pregnancy. She asks whether she needs treatment. Based on the framework described in this review, how should you approach this decision?
items.quiz_answer: According to this framework, persistent hyperprolactinemia alone without clinically meaningful hypogonadism, symptoms, or tumor progression does not necessarily justify therapy. This patient, with regular menses and no symptoms, could reasonably be managed with surveillance rather than immediate dopamine agonist initiation—she would likely fall into the 'surveillance-dominant' management state pending reassessment of reproductive intent and tumor behavior.

items.title: Risk of Suboptimal Serum Sodium Correction According to Etiology in Severe Hyponatremia.
items.summary: In this retrospective study of 876 patients with severe hyponatremia (Na ≤120 mEq/L), the etiology powerfully predicted the risk of overcorrection within 24 hours. Compared to SIAD, adrenal insufficiency carried a strikingly elevated odds ratio of 5.32 (95% CI 2.29–12.4) for rapid correction (≥10 mEq/L/24h), second only to polydipsia. This has direct relevance for endocrinologists: patients presenting with hyponatremia from adrenal insufficiency are at particularly high risk of osmotic demyelination if hormone replacement is initiated without anticipatory sodium re-lowering strategies. The authors suggest that etiological assessment should inform individualized monitoring intensity and correction targets from the outset.
items.caveat: Retrospective, two-center design with inherent selection bias; etiological classification relied on chart review and may not have captured mixed etiologies consistently. The median correction rate overall was 4.8 mEq/L/24h, suggesting many patients were managed conservatively, but the rapid-corrector subgroups driving the OR estimates are smaller.
items.quiz_question: A 58-year-old woman with known primary adrenal insufficiency presents with a serum sodium of 117 mEq/L and is started on IV hydrocortisone. Six hours later, her sodium has risen to 124 mEq/L. What does this study suggest about her risk profile, and what management step should be considered?
items.quiz_answer: This study identifies adrenal insufficiency as one of the highest-risk etiologies for rapid overcorrection (OR 5.32 vs. SIAD). A 7 mEq/L rise in 6 hours places her on trajectory to exceed the safe 10 mEq/L/24h threshold. The clinician should consider proactive re-lowering with hypotonic fluids (e.g., D5W) or desmopressin to slow further correction, and increase monitoring frequency—hourly sodium checks are warranted at this stage.

items.title: Adrenocortical Carcinoma: An Exceptional Survival Span Across a Tailored Management.
items.summary: This case report documents a woman with low-grade adrenocortical carcinoma (Ki-67 15%) who survived 16 years through three open adrenalectomies, two courses of mitotane, and a pulmonary metastasectomy—declining chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and radiotherapy throughout. The case illustrates that prolonged mitotane therapy can induce primary adrenal insufficiency requiring vigilant perioperative stress-dosing, and that radical re-resection including multi-visceral en bloc resection (right adrenal, kidney, three liver segments, IVC) can be attempted in highly selected patients at experienced centers. A peak ACTH of 369 pg/mL during postoperative adrenal crisis underscores the physiological stakes of adrenal insufficiency management in this setting.
items.caveat: Single case report with no generalizability; the exceptional outcome likely reflects tumor biology (low-grade, low Ki-67) and patient selection as much as management strategy. This should not be interpreted as evidence favoring surgical re-resection over systemic therapy for most ACC patients.
items.quiz_question: A patient with recurrent ACC on long-term mitotane develops a ACTH of 369 pg/mL in the postoperative period after a third adrenalectomy. She is hemodynamically unstable despite what you believe is adequate hydrocortisone dosing. What physiological mechanism underlies this scenario, and what does it imply for perioperative management?
items.quiz_answer: Long-term mitotane induces primary adrenal insufficiency by its adrenolytic effect on the adrenal cortex, and also accelerates cortisol metabolism via CYP3A4 induction—meaning standard stress-dose hydrocortisone replacement may be insufficient. The markedly elevated ACTH reflects complete loss of adrenal reserve. Perioperative management requires higher-than-usual hydrocortisone doses, close hemodynamic monitoring, and anticipation of prolonged vasopressor needs post-tumor removal, as seen in this case where stabilization required days of vasoactive support.

items.title: A post-operative fluid restriction protocol reduces the incidence of delayed hyponatremia following trans-sphenoidal pituitary surgery.
items.summary: This prospective interventional study of 78 patients undergoing transsphenoidal surgery for pituitary neuroendocrine tumors tested a structured fluid restriction of ≤1.5 L/day from postoperative day 5 through day 14. Delayed hyponatremia occurred in 14.1% of the fluid-restricted cohort versus 36% in a historical control cohort managed without restriction (p=0.001), with no readmissions for hyponatremia in the prospective group. Mild, self-resolving hypernatremia developed in 7 patients, manageable by relaxing fluid limits. The protocol appears safe and meaningfully reduces a common, morbid post-TSS complication.
items.caveat: This is a single-center study from a tropical setting (which may affect baseline fluid dynamics and AVP physiology), and the comparator is a historical retrospective cohort rather than a concurrent randomized control group—confounding by changes in practice over time cannot be excluded. Sample size is modest at 78 patients.
items.quiz_question: A 52-year-old woman undergoes uncomplicated endoscopic transsphenoidal resection of a non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma. On postoperative day 7 she is ambulatory and eating normally. Which postoperative management strategy, supported by this study's findings, would most reduce her risk of delayed symptomatic hyponatremia over the following week?
items.quiz_answer: Implementing a structured fluid restriction of ≤1.5 L/day from postoperative day 5 through day 14, with daily intake/output monitoring and serial serum sodium checks, reduced delayed hyponatremia incidence from 36% to 14.1% and eliminated readmissions for hyponatremia in the prospective cohort.

items.title: Clinical characteristics of 28 cases of primary adrenal lymphoma.
items.summary: This retrospective cohort of 28 patients with primary adrenal diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) found that the disease predominantly affects older males (median age 62, 64% male) and typically presents with bilateral adrenal masses >4 cm, weight loss, and early primary adrenal insufficiency (PAI). Of 19 patients with ACTH/cortisol measurements, 6 (approximately 32%) demonstrated biochemical evidence of early PAI, underscoring that adrenal function is often already compromised at diagnosis. The authors emphasize that high clinical suspicion, prompt biopsy, and adrenal function testing are essential to avoid delayed diagnosis and treatment.
items.caveat: Small single-center retrospective cohort (n=28) over 11 years limits generalizability and statistical power. Endocrine evaluation was not uniformly performed in all patients, so the true prevalence of adrenal insufficiency in this population may be underestimated.
items.quiz_question: A 65-year-old man presents with 3 months of weight loss, lumbar pain, and fatigue. CT abdomen reveals bilateral adrenal masses measuring 5 and 6 cm, with no other lymphadenopathy. Morning cortisol is low at 4 µg/dL with an elevated ACTH. What diagnosis should be high on your differential, and what next step is most critical?
items.quiz_answer: Primary adrenal lymphoma (diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) should be strongly considered, as this series shows it frequently presents with bilateral large adrenal masses and early primary adrenal insufficiency in older men. Prompt adrenal biopsy for histopathology is essential to confirm the diagnosis and initiate chemotherapy, alongside glucocorticoid replacement for PAI.

items.title: Pheochromocytoma Presenting as Spontaneous Adrenal Hemorrhage in a Normotensive Patient: A Case Report.
items.summary: This case report describes a 34-year-old normotensive man who presented with acute retroperitoneal hemorrhage from a right adrenal pheochromocytoma, initially obscuring the underlying tumor on CT. The hematoma was managed conservatively, and follow-up imaging after its regression revealed a persistent enhancing adrenal lesion; biochemical evaluation then confirmed elevated plasma metanephrines, leading to the correct diagnosis and successful laparoscopic adrenalectomy. The case reinforces that spontaneous adrenal hemorrhage can be the sentinel event of pheochromocytoma even in the absence of hypertension, and that any residual adrenal lesion after hematoma resolution warrants biochemical and functional workup.
items.caveat: Single case report; no systematic data on frequency of pheochromocytoma as the underlying etiology of spontaneous adrenal hemorrhage. Clinical guidance must be extrapolated with caution.
items.quiz_question: A 34-year-old normotensive man presents to the ED with sudden severe right flank pain. CT shows a large right retroperitoneal hemorrhage involving the adrenal gland. He is managed conservatively and repeat CT at 8 weeks shows hematoma regression but a persistent 3-cm enhancing right adrenal nodule. What is the next essential diagnostic step?
items.quiz_answer: Biochemical screening for catecholamine excess—specifically plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urine fractionated metanephrines—is essential. As illustrated in this case, pheochromocytoma can present as spontaneous adrenal hemorrhage even without hypertension, and the underlying tumor may only become apparent after the hematoma resolves. Functional evaluation must not be skipped before any planned surgical intervention.

items.title: Adrenal Infections: An Underrecognized Cause of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency.
items.summary: This review proposes a structured diagnostic algorithm for infectious causes of primary adrenal insufficiency (PAI), highlighting that M. tuberculosis and Histoplasma capsulatum are the most common culprits, though CMV and SARS-CoV-2 have also been implicated. CT typically shows bilateral adrenal lesions with central necrosis, peripheral rim enhancement, and calcifications in active disease, evolving to atrophy with persistent calcifications in chronic/TB cases. The authors emphasize that PAI prevalence in these infections ranges widely (14–100% depending on cohort and criteria), underscoring that tissue biopsy remains the definitive diagnostic tool. Management requires dual-track treatment: pathogen-directed antimicrobials plus glucocorticoid (and when indicated, mineralocorticoid) replacement, with longitudinal hormonal surveillance even in those with preserved adrenal reserve at presentation.
items.caveat: This is a narrative review without systematic search methodology or meta-analytic pooling; the very wide prevalence range (14–100%) reflects marked heterogeneity in study populations and diagnostic criteria, limiting firm conclusions.
items.quiz_question: A 42-year-old immigrant from a TB-endemic country presents with fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation, and hyponatremia. CT abdomen reveals bilateral adrenal masses with central hypodensity, peripheral rim enhancement, and calcifications. Morning cortisol is 4 µg/dL with an inadequate stimulation test. What are the two essential parallel management steps, and what imaging feature would you expect if this is longstanding/late-phase TB adrenalitis?
items.quiz_answer: The two essential steps are (1) antituberculous therapy directed at M. tuberculosis and (2) glucocorticoid (and mineralocorticoid) replacement for established PAI. In late-phase TB adrenalitis, the adrenal glands progressively shrink and become atrophic, often with persistent calcifications replacing the earlier pattern of enlargement and rim enhancement.

items.title: Excess mortality in radiotherapy-treated pituitary adenoma patients: 50-year follow-up.
items.summary: This landmark 50-year follow-up of 426 pituitary adenoma patients treated with radiotherapy at the Royal Marsden (1962–1994) found substantially elevated all-cause mortality (SMR 1.8), with cerebrovascular disease as the dominant contributor (SMR 4.9, AER 61.4 per 10,000 person-years). Endocrine/metabolic disease (SMR 5.6) and mental/behavioral disorders (SMR 5.0) were also major excess-mortality drivers. Critically, both all-cause and cerebrovascular mortality showed a dose-response relationship with radiotherapy dose, and mortality was higher in those who received combined surgery plus radiotherapy. The authors call for long-term vascular risk factor surveillance and caution regarding radiotherapy dose, while noting that whether modern high-precision techniques reduce this risk remains unknown.
items.caveat: This is a historical cohort using radiotherapy techniques from 1962–1994 that are substantially different from contemporary stereotactic radiosurgery and fractionated conformal RT; direct extrapolation to modern practice requires caution. Endocrine deficiency data and its contribution to mortality are not granularly reported.
items.quiz_question: A 55-year-old woman treated 20 years ago with conventional radiotherapy for a non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma after incomplete surgical resection presents for routine follow-up. Beyond pituitary hormone axis surveillance, what vascular risk area deserves particular proactive attention based on this long-term outcome data, and what dose-related relationship should inform your counseling?
items.quiz_answer: Cerebrovascular disease surveillance and aggressive management of vascular risk factors (hypertension, dyslipidemia, smoking, glycemia) are warranted, given the markedly elevated cerebrovascular SMR of 4.9 observed in this cohort. The dose-response relationship between radiotherapy dose and cerebrovascular mortality means patients who received higher doses or combined surgery-plus-RT are at greatest excess risk and merit the most proactive vascular monitoring.

items.title: Surveillance intensity influences the observed incidence of delayed hyponatremia after microscopic transsphenoidal pituitary surgery: early sodium and sex as risk stratifiers.
items.summary: In 285 consecutive adults undergoing microscopic transsphenoidal surgery, the apparent incidence of delayed postoperative hyponatremia (POD 3–10) varied more than threefold—from 16% in the primary cohort to 57.5% among those with a day-7 sodium measurement—with patients tested on days 5–7 having 11-fold higher odds of a recorded event. Approximately 83% of an apparent two-decade rise in incidence was attributable to increased surveillance intensity rather than true biological change. Female sex was independently associated with delayed hyponatremia (adjusted OR 2.73), with a significant age-by-sex interaction; early postoperative hyponatremia (days 0–2) carried a nearly 4-fold relative risk for later delayed hyponatremia. The authors suggest these variables could inform risk-stratified day-5–7 monitoring rather than universal post-operative sodium screening.
items.caveat: Single-center, single-surgeon retrospective study using microscopic (not endoscopic) technique, limiting generalizability. The multivariable model for early sodium as a predictor did not reach significance in the surveillance-complete subgroup (adjusted OR 2.83; 95% CI 0.86–9.33), and the exploratory risk model's AUC of 0.645 is inadequate for clinical deployment without prospective validation.
items.quiz_question: After uncomplicated transsphenoidal resection of a pituitary macroadenoma, a 38-year-old woman has a serum sodium of 133 mmol/L on postoperative day 1. Based on this study's findings, how does this early result inform her subsequent sodium surveillance strategy, and what additional demographic factor further elevates her risk of delayed hyponatremia?
items.quiz_answer: Early postoperative hyponatremia (any sodium <135 mmol/L on days 0–2) was associated with a nearly 4-fold relative risk for delayed hyponatremia (days 3–10), making this patient a candidate for targeted day-5–7 sodium follow-up rather than assuming resolution. Her female sex is independently associated with delayed hyponatremia (adjusted OR 2.73), compounding her risk and further supporting close surveillance in that window.

items.title: Diagnostic Performance of Common Biochemical Screening Tests for Mild Autonomous Cortisol Secretion in Adrenal Incidentalomas: A Systematic Review and Hierarchical SROC Meta-analysis.
items.summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 studies (1,420 patients) found that serum dexamethasone suppression testing (DST) had the highest sensitivity (97.9%) and the lowest negative likelihood ratio (0.03) among available screening tests for mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) in adrenal incidentalomas, supporting its use as a rule-out tool. Salivary DST (sensitivity 74.9%) and late-night salivary cortisol (sensitivity 62.7%) performed more modestly, while urinary free cortisol estimates were too imprecise to interpret reliably. Importantly, substantial threshold heterogeneity and indirect comparisons preclude declaring any single test diagnostically superior, and positive results require clinical contextualization and confirmatory workup.
items.caveat: All three serum DST studies used reference definitions that incorporated a dexamethasone-suppression criterion, creating incorporation bias that artificially inflates apparent sensitivity. The sparse study count (n=12) and heterogeneous MACS definitions limit generalizability of the pooled estimates.
items.quiz_question: A 58-year-old woman has a 2.2 cm right adrenal incidentaloma. You order a 1-mg overnight DST and her morning cortisol is 1.2 mcg/dL. Based on this meta-analysis, how should you interpret this result, and is further biochemical evaluation warranted?
items.quiz_answer: A suppressed cortisol after 1-mg overnight DST carries a very low negative likelihood ratio (0.03 in this meta-analysis), making MACS highly unlikely — this result effectively rules out the diagnosis in most clinical contexts. No further biochemical evaluation for autonomous cortisol secretion is warranted in this patient, though routine incidentaloma imaging follow-up per guidelines still applies.
